Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/upgrade

# Upgrade

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

`pocketone upgrade` replaces the `pocketone` executable with the latest PocketOne release and keeps the old one beside
it as `<name>-<version>` (for example `pocketone-0.0.3`), so a project can keep running the engine it was built with.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Upgrade is built into `pocketone`: the `upgrade` command is always there. There's nothing to turn on.

In your own Go build, register the command before the app starts:

```go
import "github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/upgrade"

app := pocketbase.New()
upgrade.MustRegister(app, app.RootCmd, upgrade.Config{})
app.Start()
```

## Configure

Nothing to configure: no `pocketone.yaml` section, no environment variables, no settings screens. The command has one
flag:

| Flag | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--backup` | `true` | Back up `pb_data` after upgrading, if the current folder has one. `--backup=false` skips it. |
| `--yes`, `-y` | `false` | Move from a stable release to a prerelease without asking. |

## Use

Run it from your project folder:

```bash
pocketone upgrade
```

It:

1. Picks the newest release on GitHub that fits what you're running, and stops if you already have it:
   - The newest release is offered, prereleases included: `0.1.0-alpha.2` goes to `0.1.0-alpha.3` or `0.1.0`,
     whichever is newest.
   - **From one prerelease to the next** (or to a stable release), it just upgrades.
   - **From a stable release to a prerelease** (`0.1.0` to `0.1.1-alpha.1`), it asks first. No means the newest stable
     release instead, if there's a newer one. `--yes` answers yes for you; with no answer (no terminal), it's no.
   - A local build upgrades to the newest release without asking.
2. Downloads the archive for your platform and checks it against the release's `checksums.txt` before touching
   anything.
3. Renames the current executable to `<name>-<version>` and puts the new one in its place. **Old copies are never
   deleted**, so `pocketone-0.0.3 serve` still runs a project on that version. A local build with no release version
   is kept as `<name>.old`, which the next such upgrade replaces.
4. Backs up `pb_data`, when the current folder has one, as `@upgrade_<tag>.zip` in PocketBase's backups.
5. Prints the new version, where the old one was kept, and the release notes.

Two cases where it does something else:

- **Installed with Homebrew:** it prints `brew upgrade pocketone` instead. Homebrew keeps the previous version until
  `brew cleanup`.
- **In a Docker container:** it refuses; upgrade the image instead.

It needs write access to the folder the executable is in.

A kept executable doesn't undo migrations: once a newer version has served a `pb_data`, an older one may not open it.
The backup is the way back for that.

## Integrations

Nothing integrates with it yet. Other tools can reuse its release code:

- **Custom builds** that publish their own releases set `Owner`, `Repo`, `ArchivePrefix` and `ArchiveExecutable` in
  `upgrade.Config`. Release archives are named `<prefix>_<version>_<os>_<arch>.zip`, with a goreleaser-style
  `checksums.txt` in the same release.
- **Go API.** `Config.FetchReleases(ctx)` lists the published releases, prereleases included, and
  `upgrade.UpgradeFor(current, releases, stableOnly)` picks the one to upgrade to and `upgrade.NeedsConfirm(current, release)`
  says whether to ask first. `Config.FetchRelease(ctx, tag)`
  fetches GitHub's latest stable release (tag `""`) or a given one;
  `Config.DownloadArchive(ctx, release, goos, goarch, dir)` downloads and checks a platform's archive.
  `upgrade.KeptName(exe, version)` is the name an old executable is kept under.

## Example

[`example/main.go`](example/main.go) is a PocketOne app with just the `upgrade` command. Try it with `go run ./example upgrade`.

```go
// Command example is a PocketOne app with just the upgrade command. A local build has no release version, so it is
// kept as "example.old"; release builds are kept as "<name>-<version>".
//
//	go run ./example upgrade
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/upgrade"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	upgrade.MustRegister(app, app.RootCmd, upgrade.Config{})
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## License

MIT


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/config

# Config

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

PocketOne's config file: `pocketone.yaml`, with secrets in a `.env` beside it. Put your app's settings in one file
instead of a long line of flags. Each extension has its own section in the file.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Config is built into `pocketone` and always on. Without a `pocketone.yaml`, nothing changes: every setting keeps its
default and the flags work as usual.

In your own Go build, load the file before the app is created, so its values can be the flags' defaults:

```go
cfg, err := config.Load(config.FromArgs(os.Args[1:]))
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
appCfg, _ := config.App.Get()
app := pocketbase.NewWithConfig(pocketbase.Config{DefaultDataDir: cfg.ResolvePath(appCfg.Dir)})
app.RootCmd.AddCommand(config.NewCommand(func() config.Options { return config.FromArgs(os.Args[1:]) }))
```

The module is `github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/config`. [`examples/pocketone/main.go`](../../examples/pocketone/main.go)
shows the full wiring: every `app` key as a flag default, and the `server` keys as the serve command's defaults.

## Configure

### Where the files are

- `pocketone.yaml` is looked for in the working directory, then next to the executable. `--config <path>` picks
  another file.
- The `.env` is looked for beside the config file (or in the working directory when there is no config file).
  `--env-file <path>` picks another one.
- Relative paths in the file are relative to the file's folder, so it works from any working directory.

### What goes in it

Each top-level key is one section, owned by the extension that uses it. This package owns three:

- `server`: how the app listens. `http`, `https` and `origins` are the defaults for `serve --http`, `--https` and
  `--origins`.
- `app`: your app's folders and options: the same settings as the root flags (`--dir`, `--dev`, `--hooksDir`,
  `--publicDir` and the rest), plus `env_allow`.
- `multisite`: add it only to run many instances from one binary (see [Integrations](#integrations)); `providers:
  { runtime/v1: [...] }` picks which runtimes.

```yaml
server:
  http: 127.0.0.1:8090
  origins: ["*"]
app:
  dir: ./pb_data
  hooks_dir: ./pb_hooks
  env_allow: [STRIPE_KEY]
pitr:
  retention: 168h
```

Other extensions' sections (such as `pitr` above) are described on their own pages. `pocketone config` lists every
section your binary knows.

### Flags win

A flag on the command line always wins over the file. The file only changes the defaults.

### Secrets in the .env

Write `$VAR` or `${VAR}` in any value, and keep the secret in the `.env`:

```yaml
autotls:
  dns:
    api_token: $CF_API_TOKEN
```

```bash
# .env
CF_API_TOKEN=abc123
```

- A name is looked up in the `.env` first, then in the process environment. `$$` is a literal `$`.
- A name that is set nowhere stops the app at startup, with the missing names listed.
- The `.env` takes `KEY=VALUE` lines. Blank lines, `# comments` and an `export ` prefix are fine. Quote a value to keep
  its spaces; double quotes also understand `\n`, `\t`, `\"` and `\\`.
- The `.env` is used only for these references. It is never put in the process environment, so your JS hooks
  (`$os.getenv`) don't see it, unless you list a name in `app.env_allow`.

### pocketone.yaml reference

#### `app:`

The single app: data dir, dev mode, encryption, hooks, migrations, public dir, and the .env names it may read (env_allow). Not used on a multisite host.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dir` | string |  | The data folder (pb_data). Default: pb_data next to the executable. The --dir flag wins. |
| `dev` | bool |  | Dev mode: logs and SQL statements printed to the console. The --dev flag wins. |
| `encryption_env` | string |  | Name of the environment variable holding a 32-character key that encrypts the app settings. The --encryptionEnv flag wins. |
| `query_timeout` | duration |  | Default timeout for SELECT queries, such as 30s. The --queryTimeout flag wins. |
| `hooks_dir` | string |  | The JS hooks folder. Default: pb_hooks next to pb_data. The --hooksDir flag wins. |
| `hooks_watch` | bool |  | Restart the app when a pb_hooks file changes. On unless false. The --hooksWatch flag wins. |
| `jsvm` | string |  | The JS engine for pb_hooks and pb_migrations: quickjs (PocketOne's, the default) or goja (PocketBase's own, for pure PocketBase compatibility: pages, $mcp, $tokens and JS contracts are off). The --jsvm flag wins. |
| `hooks_pool` | int |  | Only with jsvm: goja: how many JS runtimes are kept ready for hooks. Default 15. The --hooksPool flag wins. |
| `migrations_dir` | string |  | The migrations folder. Default: pb_migrations next to pb_data. The --migrationsDir flag wins. |
| `automigrate` | bool |  | Write a migration file when you change collections in the dashboard. On unless false. The --automigrate flag wins. |
| `public_dir` | string |  | The static files folder. Default: pb_public next to the executable. The --publicDir flag wins. |
| `index_fallback` | bool |  | Serve index.html for a missing static path, for single-page apps. On unless false. The --indexFallback flag wins. |
| `env_allow` | list of string |  | Names from the .env the app and its JS hooks may read. Default none. |

#### `server:`

How the binary listens: http, https and CORS origins (single-app mode: the serve command's defaults).

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `http` | string |  | Plain HTTP address, such as 127.0.0.1:8090. Single app: the --http default (the flag wins). Many instances: redirects to https when https is set. |
| `https` | string |  | HTTPS address. Single app: the --https default (the flag wins). Many instances: the main address. |
| `origins` | list of string |  | Allowed CORS origins. Single app: the --origins default (the flag wins). |
| `plain` | list of string |  | Many instances only: extra plain HTTP addresses with no redirect. |
| `tls.cert` | string |  | Many instances only: the certificate file, reloaded when it changes. |
| `tls.key` | string |  | Many instances only: the private key file, reloaded when it changes. |
| `shutdown_timeout` | duration |  | Many instances only: how long in-flight requests get to finish at stop. |

## Use

### See every section

```bash
pocketone config
```

It prints each section with its description and defaults, as YAML you can copy into your file. For the same list as
JSON (each section's name, description, owning extension, and each key with its type and default):

```bash
pocketone config --json
```

### Check your file

```bash
pocketone config check
```

It reads the file and the `.env` and reports problems, or a line like:

```
/srv/app/pocketone.yaml: ok (3 sections), secrets from /srv/app/.env
```

With no file it says `no config file: defaults only`.

### What stops startup

The app won't start, and says why, when the file has:

- a top-level key no extension in the binary owns (usually a typo); the error lists the sections it knows;
- the same section twice;
- a value that doesn't fit its key (for example text where a number goes);
- a `$VAR` that is set in neither the `.env` nor the environment.

An empty section (`pitr:` with nothing after it) is allowed and means all defaults.

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| Every extension with a section | Each extension declares its own section; its values become that extension's defaults or flag defaults. [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr), [S3 Redirect](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3redirect) and [Auto TLS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/autotls) are examples. |
| [Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker) and [Docker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/docker) | Add a `multisite` section and `pocketone serve` runs many instances instead of one app, on the runtimes `providers: { runtime/v1: [...] }` picks (default: every configured one). The `app` section and `env_allow` don't apply then; each instance has its own folder under its runtime's root. |

### The server section with many instances

On a multisite host, `server` has a few more keys: `https` is the main address, `http` then redirects plain HTTP to it
(`http` alone serves plain HTTP), `plain` lists extra plain-HTTP addresses with no redirect, `tls` names a certificate
and key file (reloaded when they change), and `shutdown_timeout` limits how long in-flight requests get at stop.

```yaml
multisite: {}
server:
  https: ":443"
  http: ":80"
  plain: [":8080"]
  tls: { cert: /etc/certs/cert.pem, key: /etc/certs/key.pem }
```

### Give your extension a section

Declare it in your own package with a typed key and defaults:

```go
type Config struct {
	Limit int `yaml:"limit" doc:"Requests per minute. The --limit flag wins."`
}

var Section = extkit.NewSection("firewall", Config{Limit: 60}, "Request limits for the app.")

cfg, found := firewall.Section.Get()   // the defaults with the file's values applied
cfg, err := firewall.Section.Require() // fails when the file doesn't have the section
```

- An extension reads a section only through its owner's key, so it can read only sections from packages it imports.
  There is no lookup by name and no access to the raw file.
- The `doc:"…"` tag on each field describes the key in `pocketone config --json` and in the key table on
  pocketone.dev.
- `config.Load` checks every section when the app starts, so a bad value fails early.

## Example

Config is built into `pocketone`: [`examples/pocketone/main.go`](../../examples/pocketone/main.go) loads `pocketone.yaml` with it before the app starts and adds the `config` command.

## Go API

- `config.FromArgs(args)` reads `--config` and `--env-file` before the full flag parse.
- `config.Load(opts)` finds, reads and checks the files, and makes them the source for every section.
  `config.Read(opts)` does the same without checking or installing them.
- `(*Config).ResolvePath(p)` makes a relative path from the file absolute, relative to the file's folder.
- `(*Config).AllowEnv(names)` copies those `.env` values into the process environment (what `app.env_allow` does).
- `config.Describe()` returns every section with its keys, types, defaults and docs (the data behind `--json`).
- `config.NewCommand(opts)` is the `config` command.

## License

MIT


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm

# JSVM

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

PocketOne's JS engine for `pb_hooks` and `pb_migrations`. It runs the same JS API as PocketBase (`$app`, `onX`,
`routerAdd`, `cronAdd`, `$http`, `$security`, ...) on QuickJS, with one VM per app:

- **Real globals.** Every hook file runs in the app's one global scope, so top-level helpers, constants and state are
  visible to every handler. No more `require()` inside each handler.
- **ES modules.** `*.pb.mjs` (and TypeScript `*.pb.ts`/`*.pb.mts`) hook files and modules use `import`/`export`,
  including top-level `await`; `*.pb.js` and `*.pb.cjs` stay scripts with `require()`. Both share the same module
  instances.
- **TypeScript.** `.ts`, `.mts` and `.cts` hooks, migrations and modules run directly (types stripped by esbuild,
  linked into the binary), with error positions in your `.ts` source.
- **Async.** Handlers can be `async`. Every Go function has an `.async(...)` twin that runs off the VM and returns a
  promise, so one app serves other requests while it waits: `await $app.findRecordById.async("posts", id)`.
- **Hard limits per app.** A memory cap (JS heap plus Go objects JS holds), a CPU and a wall-clock budget per task, and
  caps on queued tasks and async calls. A runaway script stops with an error; other apps in the process keep running.
- **Real error positions.** Stack traces name `pb_hooks/<file>:<line>`.

The `pocketone` binary and every Pocker instance run on it. PocketBase's own `plugins/jsvm` (goja) is for pure
PocketBase compatibility only: `jsvm: goja` under `app:` in `pocketone.yaml` (or `--jsvm goja`) runs a single app on it,
with pages, `$mcp`, `$tokens`, `$bulkmail` and JS contracts off.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

The engine is pure Go (QuickJS translated to Go by [modernc.org/libquickjs](https://pkg.go.dev/modernc.org/libquickjs),
the way PocketBase uses modernc.org/sqlite), so it needs no cgo: `CGO_ENABLED=0` builds and cross-compiles work as with
stock PocketBase. In your own Go build, register it where you'd register `plugins/jsvm`:

```go
jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks", MigrationsDir: "pb_migrations"})
```

The module is `github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm`.

## Configure

`Config` takes PocketBase's jsvm fields (`HooksDir`, `HooksWatch`, `HooksFilesPattern`, `MigrationsDir`,
`MigrationsFilesPattern`, `TypesDir`; `HooksPoolSize` is accepted and ignored) plus:

- `OnInit func(rt js.Runtime)`: add globals after everything else is set up.
- `VM`: the limits. `MemoryLimit` (default 64 MiB), `TaskBudget` (JS time per task, default 5 s), `TaskWall` (wall time
  per task, Go calls included, default 30 s), `QueueSize`, `MaxAsync`, `MaxPumpDepth`.
  Array methods that walk every index (`join`, `indexOf`, `slice`, `forEach`, `concat`, `flat`, ...) and arrays passed
  to Go throw a `RangeError` past `MemoryLimit / 16` elements: QuickJS doesn't check `TaskBudget` inside those loops,
  and a sparse array (`new Array(1e9)`) or array-like costs no memory, so the cap is what stops them. No dense array
  that long fits in `MemoryLimit`.
- `Extensions`: values that extend it (below).

## Use

Write hooks and migrations as in PocketBase's [JS docs](https://pocketbase.io/docs/js-overview/); they run unchanged.
What's new:

```js
// pb_hooks/main.pb.js
const cache = new Map()

routerAdd("GET", "/post/{slug}", async (e) => {
	const slug = e.request.pathValue("slug")
	if (!cache.has(slug)) {
		cache.set(slug, await e.app.findFirstRecordByData.async("posts", "slug", slug))
	}
	return e.json(200, cache.get(slug))
})
```

- Globals live as long as the app's VM. A restart, a hooks reload or running out of memory starts a fresh one, so keep
  durable data in the database.
- After an `await`, other requests may have run: use `e.app`, not the global `$app`, and keep transactions short across
  `await`s (they hold SQLite's write lock).
- Calls that wait on I/O (`$app` methods, DB queries, `$http.send`, `sleep`) let the app's other requests run even
  without `.async`.
- `process.env` and a small `Buffer` (`from`, `toString` with utf8, base64, hex) are there.

### Modules: import and require

Name a file for what it is: `.mjs` is an ES module, `.cjs` is CommonJS. A plain `.js` file is CommonJS, so existing
PocketBase hooks run unchanged (inside `node_modules`, Node's rule applies: `"type": "module"` in the package's
`package.json` makes its `.js` files ES modules). TypeScript is written as ES modules, so `.ts` and `.mts` are ES
modules and `.cts` is the CommonJS exception.

| File | Runs as | Shares through |
|---|---|---|
| `pb_hooks/*.pb.mjs`, `*.pb.ts`, `*.pb.mts` | ES module: `import`, `export`, top-level `await`, `import.meta` | `export` / `import`; its top-level names are private |
| `pb_hooks/*.pb.js`, `*.pb.cjs`, `*.pb.cts` | script in the app's one global scope, with `require()` | globals |
| `pb_migrations/*.mjs`, `*.ts`, `*.mts` | ES module | each migration has its own scope either way |
| `pb_migrations/*.js`, `*.cjs`, `*.cts` | script in its own function scope | |

All of them run in the app's one VM: scripts and modules share the global object (a module can read a script's
globals) and one instance of every module.

```js
// pb_hooks/lib/store.mjs
export const state = { hits: 0 }
export const bump = () => ++state.hits

// pb_hooks/main.pb.mjs
import { bump } from "./lib/store.mjs"
import legacy from "./lib/legacy.cjs"      // CommonJS: module.exports is the default export
import { hello } from "some-package"       // node_modules, CommonJS or ES
const posts = await $app.findCollectionByNameOrId.async("posts")  // top-level await: done before the app serves

routerAdd("GET", "/hit", (e) => e.json(200, { hits: bump() }))
```

- `import` and `require()` resolve the same way: relative paths (`.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.json` and `index.*`
  tried in turn), then `node_modules` packages by `package.json` `exports` (the `import` or `require` condition) or
  `main`.
- A module loads once per app, however many files import or require it, so its state is shared by every request.
  Importing a CommonJS module gives its `module.exports` as the default export, its keys as named exports, and the same
  instance `require()` returns.
- `require()` of an ES module returns its namespace (the same instance `import` gives), as in Node 22, as long as the
  module has no top-level `await`; for one that does, use `await import("./lib/x.mjs")`.

### TypeScript

`.ts`, `.mts` and `.cts` files run as they are: esbuild strips the types when the file loads, and each file's source
map is kept, so an error names `pb_hooks/main.pb.mts:12:5` in your source, not in the stripped code.

- There's no type checking at runtime. Check with `tsc --noEmit` or your editor; `pb_data/types.d.ts` types the
  whole JS API.
- Imports may name the compiled file, as TypeScript's `NodeNext` style does: `import { add } from "./math.js"` loads
  `math.ts` when there's no `math.js`.
- `import type` and other type-only imports disappear, so a `*.pb.cts` script can use them and stay a script.
- A `.cts` module may still be written with `import`/`export`; it's turned into CommonJS.

### Types

When the app starts, `pb_data/types.d.ts` gets the declarations of the whole JS API, for your editor and `tsc`:

- PocketBase's API generated from PocketOne's core (its extra hooks included), by PocketBase's own generator.
- What this engine adds ([`pocketone.d.ts`](pocketone.d.ts)): `.async` on every Go function, fully typed
  (`await $app.findRecordById.async(...)` is a `Promise<core.Record>`), `require`, `process`, `Buffer`, `console`,
  `import.meta`.
- Each extension's own API, for the extensions on in that app (`$mcp`, `$tokens`, `$bulkmail`, `onContracts` and
  the contracts' action hooks).

To type-check, point a `tsconfig.json` at it:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": { "target": "ES2022", "module": "ESNext", "moduleResolution": "Bundler", "lib": ["ES2022"],
    "strict": true, "noEmit": true, "allowImportingTsExtensions": true, "skipLibCheck": true },
  "include": ["pb_data/types.d.ts", "pb_hooks/**/*", "pb_migrations/**/*"]
}
```

`skipLibCheck` skips two type errors inside PocketBase's own generated declarations. In a PocketOne checkout,
`go generate` in `ext/jsvm` regenerates the declarations after a core change (the `TestTypes` tests fail until you
do).

## Integrations

Extensions plug in through `Config.Extensions` with the engine-neutral types in
[`ext/extkit/js`](../extkit/js/js.go). A value implements any of:

- `OnInit(rt)`: set up the VM. `BindJS(app, rt)`: expose a Go API. `TypeScript()`: declare it for editors and
  `tsc` (appended to `pb_data/types.d.ts`).
- `OnCall(rt)`: wrap every handler call; an error refuses it.
- `HTTPClient(rt)`: the client `$http.send` uses.
- `HookFiles`, `MigrationFiles`, `Modules`: hooks, migrations and `require()` modules from somewhere other than disk.
- `OnLoad(rt, root, file, content)`: wrap loading each hook file.

`js.Run(app, fn)` runs Go code on the app's VM; a `js.Func` kept from JS can be called from any goroutine.

[Bundle](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bundle) uses these to serve hooks and migrations embedded in the binary.

## Example

```go
// Command example serves example/pb_hooks with the jsvm extension: one QuickJS VM for the app, so the hook file's
// top-level helpers and state are visible to every handler.
//
//	cd example && go run . serve
//	curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hello/world
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app)
	jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks", MigrationsDir: "pb_migrations"})
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## How it works

- Each app's VM is owned by one goroutine, its loop; everything that touches the VM runs there. Go code
  elsewhere posts tasks and waits. A Go call made from JS that fires a hook runs it inline, so Go → JS → Go → JS works.
- Go values cross live through two QuickJS classes: `GoObject` (property get/set/has/keys go to Go by reflection, with
  PocketBase's JS names) and `GoFunc` (calls go to Go). Each holds a handle into the VM's table; QuickJS's refcounting
  frees it as soon as JS drops it.
- Memory: QuickJS caps its own heap. Go objects JS holds are charged to the same budget: a per-type estimate, and a
  reachability walk for fresh results of Go calls.
- QuickJS is [modernc.org/libquickjs](https://pkg.go.dev/modernc.org/libquickjs), Bellard's QuickJS translated to Go,
  so there is no cgo. It runs about as fast as goja; deep recursion stops at `VM.StackSize` (QuickJS stack slots,
  about one per call; default 5000) with "InternalError: stack overflow".
- Benchmarks and the red team (27 attacks against 50 VMs in one process) are in the package's tests
  (`ASYNCVM_BENCH=1`, `ASYNCVM_REDTEAM=1`).

## License

MIT


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker

# Pocker

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

Many PocketOne instances in one process (like Docker, but for PocketOne), routed by hostname. Each instance is a
normal app folder and starts on its first request, in tens of milliseconds. Pocker provides
[runtime/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/runtime/v1) for [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite); its peer [Docker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/docker) runs each instance in a container instead.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Pocker is built into `pocketone`. Add a `multisite` section to `pocketone.yaml` and `pocketone serve` hosts many
instances instead of one app, with pocker as the runtime (docker too, when it has its `docker` section):

```yaml
multisite: {}
```

In your own Go build, add it to the host's extensions ([`examples/pocketone/multi.go`](../../examples/pocketone/multi.go)
is the stock binary's version), or run a `pocker.Server` on its own as [the example](#example) does:

```go
h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath, Extensions: []multisite.Extension{
	&pocker.Provider{
		Resolve:  cfg.ResolvePath,
		Standard: standard.New(), // every instance gets the standard set (tokens, mcp, pitr, ...)
		Extensions: []pocker.Extension{
			myextension.New(), // your own PocketOne extensions, on every instance too
		},
	},
}})
```

The module is `github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/pocker`.

## Configure

The `pocker` section sets where instances live, the JS pool, outbound network and the default limits for every
instance (keys below). Listeners, instances and the firewall are the [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) sections (`server`,
`instances`, `firewall`).

```yaml
multisite: {}
instances: { file: ./instances.yaml }
pocker:
  root: ./pb_root           # one folder per instance: <root>/<id>
  hooks_pool_size: 2
  egress_allow: []          # private networks instances may still reach
  max_js_execution: 30s     # default limits; each instance can override them
  max_js_allocation: 64MiB
```

An instance overrides any limit in its own `limits` (missing fields keep the default):

```yaml
instances:
  - id: shop
    hosts: [shop.example.com]
    limits: { max_js_execution: 60s, max_concurrent_js: 32 }
```

Every instance runs the PocketOne code in the binary; an instance's `version` is ignored.

### pocketone.yaml reference

#### `pocker:`

Runtime provider pocker: instances run in-process (root folder, hooks pool, egress allow list, instance limit defaults).

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `root` | string | `./pb_root` | The folder holding one folder per instance: <root>/<id>. |
| `hooks_pool_size` | int | `2` | Ignored: each instance has one JS VM (ext/jsvm). Kept so existing configs load. |
| `max_js_execution` | duration | `30s` | Longest any single JS call (hook, route, cron job, migration) may run. |
| `max_js_allocation` | int | `67108864` | Largest result a JS built-in may allocate in one step, such as 64MiB. |
| `max_call_stack_size` | int | `2000` | Deepest JS recursion allowed. |
| `max_sleep` | duration | `10s` | Longest a JS sleep() call may wait. |
| `max_query_duration` | duration | `30s` | Longest an SQL statement without its own deadline may run. |
| `http_send_max_timeout` | duration | `1m0s` | Longest timeout a JS $http.send call may use. |
| `http_send_max_body` | int | `10485760` | Largest response body a JS $http.send call may read, such as 10MiB. |
| `max_concurrent_js` | int | `16` | JS calls an instance runs at once; more wait up to max_js_execution, then fail. |
| `egress_allow` | list of string |  | Private networks (CIDRs) instances may still connect to. Default none: public addresses only. |

## Use

### Try it with any hostname

```yaml
# pocketone.yaml
server: { http: "127.0.0.1:8090" }
multisite: {}
instances: { dev: true }
pocker: { root: ./pb_root }
```

```sh
pocketone serve
curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/health   # creates and serves ./pb_root/blog.localhost
```

In dev mode a hostname no instance maps becomes an instance named after it, its folder is made on first use, and it
runs in dev mode. In production only the hostnames in the instances file are served (see
[Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite#the-instances-file)).

### Each instance

- A normal app folder, `<root>/<id>`: `pb_data`, `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations`, `pb_public`. Its dashboard is at
  `https://<its hostname>/_/`.
- Its JS hooks see only its own `secrets`, through `$os.getenv` and `process.env`.
- A change to its `secrets`, `encryption_key`, `access`, `limits`, `dev`, `dir`, `superusers`, `private`, `extensions` or `remote`
  restarts its app on the next request, after in-flight requests finish. A hostname change doesn't restart it.
- A change in `pb_hooks` restarts just that instance. A broken hooks file affects only that instance (below).

### Broken hook files

In dev mode, a `pb_hooks` file that fails to load is logged and skipped, and the rest of the instance runs, so you can
fix it live. Otherwise an instance doesn't start with a broken file.

When a running instance's `pb_hooks` change, the new code starts beside the running app and takes over only once it
has started. If it fails to load, the previous code keeps serving and the error goes to the instance log, so a bad
edit never takes a working instance down.

### Logs

The app's own logs (the dashboard's Logs) are per instance, in its `pb_data`. `console.*` from JS hooks goes to
`<instance>/logs/exec.log` as JSON lines (`message`, `stream`, `time`), rotated to `exec.log.1` at 10 MiB. A start
failure is written there too.

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) | Routing, listeners, instances file and gates. Pocker is one of its runtimes (runtime/v1). |
| [Sandbox](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/sandbox) | Every instance's JS hooks, SQL and outbound network run in it, so one instance can't reach another or the host. |
| [Firewall](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/firewall) | Peer allow-list and rate limits in front of every instance; per-instance limits in `extensions.firewall`. |
| [Auto TLS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/autotls) | In the stock binary: certificates for the hostnames instances map (`autotls` section). |
| [Server Timing](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/servertiming) | In the stock binary: Server-Timing headers on every response. |
| [Mailtrap](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mailtrap) | In the stock binary: dev instances with SMTP off send mail to a local inbox. |
| [Edge](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/edge) | Instances another edge runs are forwarded there instead of started here. |
| [Stats](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/stats) | Measures disk use and last request for each instance under `root`. |
| PocketOne extensions | In your own build, any extension such as [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr), [S3 Fallback](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3-fallback) or [Mail Relay](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mailrelay) runs on every instance, and an instance's `extensions.<name>` settings override the extension's defaults. `enabled: false` turns it off for that instance. |

### Building on Pocker

- **Standard set (required).** `pocker.Provider.Standard` (or `pocker.Server.Standard`, `ManagerOptions.Standard`) is
  [ext/standard](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/standard)'s set, and Pocker won't start an instance without it: a server without one
  refuses to run, so no host can make an instance that lacks the standard extensions. Every instance gets its members, each turned off per instance with `extensions.<name>.enabled: false`, and its
  startup lines (`standard: on: ...`) are in the instance's own log. Listing a member in `Extensions` too is an error.
- **Contracts the host provides.** `Server.Host` (or `Provider.Host`) is the host's contract scope. A contract the
  host provides for its instances steps aside inside each instance's app, and the host answers it on the instance's
  hostname in `Server.InstanceRoutes` (or `Provider.InstanceRoutes`, `ManagerOptions.InstanceRoutes`): after the
  gates and the blocked answer, before the app. `pocker.Remote(m, host)` is remote/v1 for Pocker instances (restart
  through the Manager, logs from `logs/exec.log`); add your own auth:

  ```go
  host := extkit.NewScope("multisite")
  srv.Host = host
  srv.OnStart = func(m *pocker.Manager) { remotev1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(host, pocker.Remote(m, host)) }
  srv.InstanceRoutes = append(srv.InstanceRoutes, func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
  	return remotev1.W.HostHandler(host, multisite.InstanceID, myAuth, next)
  })
  ```

  deploy/v1 works the same way with `deploy.New(...)` as the handler: `deployv1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(host,
  ...)` and `extkit.HostRoutes(host, deployv1.Contract, multisite.InstanceID, next)` as an instance route.
- **Extensions.** `pocker.Provider.Extensions` (or `pocker.Server.Extensions`) takes any `extkit.Extension`, registered on each
  instance's app before it starts with that instance's `extensions.<name>` settings. Host-level code can implement
  `AppIniter`, `JSIniter`, `Starter`, or be a host extension (`multisite.Extension`, registered on the host like any
  other: servertiming, autotls). See
  [POCKER.md](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker/pocker#extensions).
- **Setup per instance.** `SetupApp(inst, app)` runs after migrations and before the app serves, e.g. to add a route
  checked against `inst.Private`.
- **Manager.** `OnStart` hands host code the `Manager`: `WithInstanceStopped(ctx, id, fn)` changes an instance's files
  while it's stopped (deploys, restores), `StartInstance`, `Running`, `InstanceDir`, `LogInstance`.
- **Restarts.** `app.Restart()` (a backup restore, PITR) restarts only that instance.

## Example

A Pocker build with one extension: a Go route and an admin dashboard page on every instance, in dev mode. Run it from
this folder with `go run ./example`, then open `http://blog.localhost:8090/_/` (login `admin@example.com` /
`password`).

```go
// Command pocker-extension is a Pocker build with one extension: a Go route and an admin dashboard page,
// added to every instance. See docs/extensions.md.
//
// Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password.
package main

import (
	"context"
	"embed"
	"io/fs"
	"log"
	"net/http"
	"os"
	"os/signal"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/apis"
	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/pocker"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/standard"
)

//go:embed ui
var uiFiles embed.FS

func main() {
	cfg := pocker.DefaultConfig()
	cfg.Dev = true // any hostname; drop this for production (instances.yaml required)

	ui, _ := fs.Sub(uiFiles, "ui")

	srv := &pocker.Server{
		Config:   cfg,
		Standard: standard.New(), // every instance gets the standard extensions (tokens, mcp, pages, pitr, ...)
		// Runs for every instance's app after its migrations, before it serves.
		SetupApp: func(inst pocker.Instance, app core.App) error {
			// local testing: every instance gets superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password"
			if err := devusers.Ensure(app); err != nil {
				return err
			}
			app.OnServe().BindFunc(func(se *core.ServeEvent) error {
				// a Go route, superuser only
				se.Router.GET("/api/hello", func(e *core.RequestEvent) error {
					return e.JSON(http.StatusOK, map[string]string{"instance": inst.ID})
				}).Bind(apis.RequireSuperuserAuth())

				// an admin dashboard extension: ui/main.js is loaded by the dashboard before its router starts
				se.UIExtensions = append(se.UIExtensions, core.UIExtension{Name: "hello", FS: ui})
				return se.Next()
			})
			return nil
		},
	}

	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt)
	defer stop()
	if err := srv.Run(ctx); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## Untrusted instances

Pocker runs every instance's JS hooks in the [sandbox](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/sandbox). For why that's safe enough to host code
from people you don't know, and where it isn't, see [How is this safe?](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/sandbox#how-is-this-safe).
Memory is the main limit: only one-shot allocations are capped, so a hook that grows memory slowly affects the whole
process. [POCKER.md](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker/pocker#sandbox) lists what the sandbox covers.

## Reference

[POCKER.md](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker/pocker) is the full guide: production `pocketone.yaml`, every instance field, extension interfaces, the
sandbox, PocketBase changes and versions.

## License

MIT

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker/pocker

# Pocker

Pocker hosts many PocketOne instances in one process. It is PocketOne itself (this repo tracks
[upstream PocketBase](https://ganigeorgiev.com/git/pocketbase/pocketbase) and shares its history) plus a small engine in
this folder, run by the stock `pocketone` binary as a [runtime/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/runtime/v1) provider (a `multisite`
section in pocketone.yaml).

- One port, many instances. Each request's hostname maps to a canonical instance id.
- Each instance is a normal app folder, `<root>/<id>` (`pb_data`, `pb_hooks`, `pb_migrations`, `pb_public`),
  with its own environment for JS hooks (`$os.getenv`, `process.env`), its own JS migrations and its own settings
  encryption key.
- An instance's app starts on its first request (tens of milliseconds) and keeps running.

## Dev mode: any hostname

```yaml
# pocketone.yaml
server: { http: "127.0.0.1:8090" }
multisite: {}
instances: { dev: true }
pocker: { root: ./pb_root }
```

```sh
pocketone serve
curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' http://127.0.0.1:8090/api/health   # creates and serves ./pb_root/blog.localhost
```

A hostname the instance source doesn't map uses the hostname itself as its id (lowercase, no port, no trailing dot;
anything that isn't a safe folder name gets 400), its folder is created on first use, and apps run in dev
mode. The instances file (or another source) is optional in dev mode; hosts it maps keep their own ids.

## Production: mapped hostnames only

Without dev mode, Pocker serves only what an instance source maps. The built-in source is the `instances` section's
YAML file (reloaded when it changes; the host refuses to start without it):

```yaml
# instances.yaml
instances:
  - id: blog                      # folder <root>/blog
    hosts: [blog.example.com, www.blog.example.com]
  - id: shop
    hosts: [shop.example.com]
    secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: sk_live_... }               # the app's environment
    encryption_key: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef   # encrypts the app's stored settings; not visible to JS
    access: { cors_origins: [https://shop.example.com] }
    extensions: { firewall: { trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] } }   # settings for extensions, by name
  - id: old
    hosts: [old.example.com]
    blocked: { status: 402, message: "Payment required" }
```

Unknown hosts get 404 and no folder is ever created from a request. Ids are lowercase letters, digits, dots and dashes.
Hosting platforms plug in their own [`InstanceSource`](instance.go) (for example a control plane streaming the
hostname -> id map over SSE) instead of the file; a community mothership is one (the `mothership` section,
[ext/mothership](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mothership)).

pocketone.yaml for a production host (each extension owns its section; every field has a default):

```yaml
server:
  https: ":443"
  http: ":80"               # redirects to HTTPS (and answers ACME HTTP-01 challenges)
  plain: []                 # extra plain-HTTP listeners (no TLS, no redirect), e.g. a private network other servers forward on
  tls: { cert: /path/fullchain.pem, key: /path/privkey.pem }   # re-read when they change; or the autotls section

multisite: {}
instances: { file: ./instances.yaml }

pocker:
  root: ./pb_root
  hooks_pool_size: 2
  egress_allow: []          # private networks apps may still reach (default none)
  # default limits for every instance (each instance can override them, see below)
  max_js_execution: 30s     # any single JS call (hook, route, cron, migration)
  max_js_allocation: 64MiB  # one-shot JS allocations
  max_call_stack_size: 2000
  max_sleep: 10s
  max_query_duration: 30s   # any SQL statement without its own deadline
  http_send_max_timeout: 60s
  http_send_max_body: 10MiB
  max_concurrent_js: 16     # JS calls an instance runs at once; more wait up to max_js_execution, then fail

rate_limits:                # per client IP and per instance; trusted clients get the trusted set
  ip_hourly: 1000
  instance_hourly: 10000
  ip_concurrent: 15
  instance_concurrent: 250
  file_weight: 0.1          # a /api/files request costs a tenth
  trusted: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_hourly: 20000, ip_concurrent: 50, instance_concurrent: 250 }
  # off: true               # no rate limiting (the default in dev mode unless rate_limits is set)

firewall:
  allow_cidrs: []               # peers allowed to connect (empty = everyone); others get 403
  trusted_proxies: []           # peers whose client-IP headers are believed
  client_ip_headers: [CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP]
  trusted_clients: []           # client IPs with the trusted limits on every instance
  trusted_client_headers: [X-Client-IP]   # a trusted client names its end user (own buckets)
  rate_limit_header_prefix: X-RateLimit

# autotls:                      # automatic certificates (ACME, via CertMagic, Caddy's certificate engine)
#   auto: true
#   email: ops@example.com
#   ca: letsencrypt             # letsencrypt (default), letsencrypt-staging, zerossl, or an ACME directory URL
#   storage: ./pb_root/.pocker-certs
#   domains: ["*.example.com", "example.com"]   # obtained up front; wildcards need dns
#   dns: { provider: cloudflare, api_token_env: CF_API_TOKEN }   # only needed for wildcards
```

**Firewall** ([ext/firewall](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/firewall); on whenever the config has `firewall` or `rate_limits`). Peers
outside `allow_cidrs` get 403. The client IP comes from `client_ip_headers` only when the peer is a trusted proxy,
otherwise it is the peer. Rate-limited requests get 429 with `Retry-After` and a message naming the limit; every routed
response carries `<prefix>-{Ip,Instance}-{Hourly,Concurrent}-{Limit,Remaining}` and `<prefix>-{Ip,Instance}-Hourly-Reset`,
listed in `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`. Long-lived responses (realtime) hold their concurrency slot until they end.

**TLS.** Certificate files are core (`server.tls`). Automatic certificates are [ext/autotls](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/autotls) (its
`autotls` section): with `auto: true` and no `dns`, every hostname the instance source maps gets its own certificate on
its first TLS handshake (HTTP-01 / TLS-ALPN-01), with any DNS host and no API token; hostnames no instance serves never
trigger issuance. A DNS provider (Cloudflare for now) is only needed for wildcard `domains`, proved through DNS-01; a
wildcard without one is a config error.

Each instance can override any of those limits (zero or missing fields keep the default):

```yaml
instances:
  - id: shop
    hosts: [shop.example.com]
    limits:
      max_js_execution: 60s
      max_js_allocation: 128MiB
  - id: api
    hosts: [api.example.com]
    access: { cors_origins: [https://app.example.com] }
    limits: { max_concurrent_js: 32 }
    extensions:
      firewall: { rate_limits: { ip_hourly: 5000, instance_concurrent: 500 }, trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] }
```

## Extensions

`pocker.Provider.Extensions` (or `pocker.Server.Extensions` in Go) takes extensions (see `extension.go`). Each implements `Name()` and
any of:

| Interface | Used for |
|---|---|
| `extkit.Extension` | a PocketOne extension, registered on every instance's app before it bootstraps (`Register(app, cfg)`) with the instance's `extensions.<name>` settings, its id in `extkit.AppID(app)`; e.g. [pitr](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr), [storage](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3-fallback), [tokens](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/tokens), [s3redirect](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3redirect), [mailrelay](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mailrelay), [bulkmail](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bulkmail). `enabled: false` skips it for that instance. A change to an instance's `extensions:` settings restarts its app on its next request. The same value works on a single app. |
| `multisite.Extension` | a host extension (`RegisterHost`): it provides host contracts (gate/v1, tls/v1, http.wrap/v1, ...) as on any runtime ([docs/extensions.md](https://pocketone.dev/docs/writing-an-extension#host-extensions)) |
| `Starter` | background work that needs pocker's Manager |
| `AppIniter` | host code that needs the whole `Instance` when setting up its app (`InitApp(inst, app)`); runs on every start, including restarts. Extensions use `extkit.Extension` instead, so they run on a single app too and pass the [conformance test](https://github.com/pockethost/pocketone/blob/main/ext/extkit/conformance/conformance.go). |

Per-instance settings for an extension go under the instance's `extensions.<name>` (read them with `pocker.DecodeExtensionConfig`).
`app.Restart()` (a backup restore, pitr) restarts only that instance, not the process.
Timings for the Server-Timing header are registered with `multisite.Timing(ctx, fn)`. The stock `pocketone` binary runs
pocker with [mailtrap](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mailtrap), and its host with [servertiming](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/servertiming) and
[autotls](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/autotls) (`multisite.Options.Extensions`, the same under docker); the
[firewall](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/firewall) turns on from its sections.

## Platform values and logs

- **Superusers** (`superusers: [{email, password_hash, id?, token_key?}]`) are upserted into the app's `_superusers`
  in Go when it starts, e.g. so a hosting platform's login works in the dashboard. Nothing goes through env.
- **Private values** (`private: {...}`) are for the host application's Go code and never visible to JS. A host
  registers that code with `Server.SetupApp(inst, app)`, which runs after migrations and before the app serves (for
  example a backup route checked against `inst.Private["backup_token"]`).
- **Secrets** (`secrets: {...}`) are the instance's environment: what its JS sees through `$os.getenv` /
  `process.env`, and nothing else. No names are reserved; platform settings are explicit fields.
- **Encryption key** (`encryption_key`) encrypts the app's stored settings (like `--encryptionEnv`). JS never sees it.
- **Access** (`access: {cors_origins}`) is the owner's say over which browser origins may call the instance
  (PocketBase matching: exact, `*`, wildcards; empty = any). Client IPs that get the trusted rate limits are the
  firewall's `extensions.firewall.trusted_ips` (on top of the process-wide `firewall.trusted_clients`).
- **Extensions** (`extensions: {<name>: ...}`) are per-instance settings for extensions; extensions read them once, so changing them restarts the app on its next request.
- **Logs:** the app's own logs (the dashboard's Logs) are per instance in its `pb_data`. `console.*` from JS hooks
  goes to `<instance>/logs/exec.log` as JSON lines `{message, stream, time}` (`stdout` for log/info/debug, `stderr`
  for warn/error), rotated to `exec.log.1` at 10 MiB. A start failure (e.g. a broken hooks file) is written there too,
  and only that instance fails.

When an instance's `secrets`, `encryption_key`, `access`, `limits`, `dev`, `dir`, `superusers`, `private` or `remote` changes, its app restarts on the next request (the old one finishes
in-flight requests first), so a rotated secret takes effect immediately. Host changes apply without a restart.

`GET /.well-known/health` on any host reports `{status, instances, running}`.

**Changing an instance's files from host code** (deploys, restores): `Manager.WithInstanceStopped(ctx, id, fn)` stops
the app, holds new requests for that instance, runs `fn(dir)`, then lets them through to a fresh app.
`Manager.StartInstance(ctx, id)` starts it right away and returns the start error (for example to tell a deploy that
a hook is broken), `Manager.Running(id)` says whether it is started, and `Manager.InstanceDir(id)` gives its folder.
`Manager.Ready()` says whether the instance list has loaded. `Manager.LogInstance(id, stream, message)` appends to the instance's `logs/exec.log` (e.g. a scheduled job's result).
Host code that runs in its own goroutines gets the Manager from `Server.OnStart`, before any request is served.

**Several servers, one set of instances.** An instance with `remote: <url>` runs on another server: Pocker checks the
peer and the instance's rate limits here, then forwards the request (a reverse proxy to the URL by default;
`Server.Forward` replaces it, e.g. to hold requests while the other server restarts). Its app never starts here, and
an app already running here stops when `remote` is set. `plain_listen` gives the other servers a plain-HTTP port on a
private network, and `Manager.Firewall()` lets host routes in front of the Manager use the same peer check.

## Sandbox

Every instance's JS hooks and migrations run in a sandbox (the [sandbox](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/sandbox) extension), and its SQL runs behind
SQLite's authorizer ([`sandbox/sqlguard.go`](../sandbox/sqlguard.go)). The sandbox extension also owns the egress policy
([`sandbox/egress.go`](../sandbox/egress.go)); pocker turns it on for its instances. [`sandbox_test.go`](sandbox_test.go) runs one attack per
route from one instance against another instance and the host; all of these are refused:

| Area | What the sandbox does |
|---|---|
| Files: `$os.*`, `$filepath.glob/walk*`, `$filesystem.fileFromPath`, `$template.loadFiles`, `$apis.static`, `require()` | Confined to the instance folder with an `os.Root`: the kernel resolves every path beneath it, refusing `..` and symlinks that leave it. Relative paths and absolute paths inside the folder (`__hooks + "/x"`) work as before. |
| Host primitives: `$os.cmd`, `$os.exec`, `$os.exit`, `$os.args`, `$filesystem.local` | Disabled (`$os.args` is empty). |
| Environment: `$os.getenv`, `process.env` | Only the instance's own `secrets`. |
| Go internals: `$app.restart/bootstrap/runAllMigrations/onServe/onTerminate/onBootstrap/cron/unsafeWithoutHooks`, `hook.bindFunc/bind/trigger/unbind*`, `*sql.DB/Conn/Tx/Stmt` (e.g. `dbx.DB.DB()`), `database/sql/driver`, `os/exec`, `net`, `syscall`, `http.Server` controls | Hidden from JS (the sandbox's member filter: they read as `undefined`, including when promoted from an embedded app type). Top-level `onRecord*`, `routerAdd`, `cronAdd` and the rest of `$app` work as usual. |
| Raw SQL (`$app.db().newQuery`) | Allowed. SQLite's authorizer refuses `ATTACH` (and `VACUUM INTO`) outside the instance's `pb_data`, `PRAGMA temp_store_directory/data_store_directory` and `load_extension`; the CLI-only `readfile`/`writefile`/`fsdir` don't exist in the library. Statements without a deadline get `max_query_duration`. |
| CPU | Every JS call is interrupted after `max_js_execution`, Go calls included; `sleep()` is capped at 10 s. At most `max_concurrent_js` calls are in flight per instance. |
| Memory | Each instance has one QuickJS VM ([ext/jsvm](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm)) with a hard cap (64 MiB by default): its JS heap plus the Go objects its JS holds. Growth past it, gradual or at once, is an out-of-memory error for that instance only. The JS stack is capped by size, so deep recursion is an error, never a crash. `$os.readFile`, `fileFromPath` and `readerToString`/`toBytes` are capped at `max_js_allocation`. |
| Outbound network: `$http.send`, `$filesystem.fileFromURL`, S3 storage and backups, OAuth2/JWK fetches, SMTP | Public addresses only, checked on the address actually connected to (after DNS, so rebinding doesn't help): loopback, private ranges, link-local and cloud metadata, CGNAT, multicast, reserved and documentation ranges, and IPv6 equivalents/IPv4-in-IPv6 are refused unless listed in `egress_allow`. Installed process-wide on Go's default HTTP transport and PocketBase's SMTP client (`pocker/egress.go`). Host code that must reach private addresses (e.g. a control plane over a private network) uses its own `http.Client` with its own transport. `$http.send` timeouts and response bodies are capped. |

**Limits of the memory controls:** Go objects JS holds are charged by estimate, and Go's garbage collector can let the
process use up to about twice the charge; set `GOMEMLIMIT` for the process as the backstop.

**Not covered yet:** per-instance concurrency limits, and OS-level defence in depth: run Pocker as a non-root user with an
OS firewall that only lets that user reach public addresses (a second, independent egress layer), plus seccomp and
Landlock.

## Changes to PocketBase

These live in the repo root (PocketBase's own files), not in this extension.

Kept small and marked `// PocketOne:` so upstream merges stay easy:

- `core.BaseAppConfig.AppMigrations`: a per-app migrations list (JS migrations from [jsvm](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm) register
  there instead of the global `core.AppMigrations`).
- `core.BaseAppConfig.EncryptionKey`: the settings encryption key passed in directly instead of read from the process
  environment.
- The JS engine isn't a core change: Pocker runs [jsvm](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm) (QuickJS), an extension, and the
  [sandbox](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/sandbox) plugs into it. PocketBase's own `plugins/jsvm` is exactly upstream's.
- Mail needs no core change: the sandbox sends an app's own SMTP through the egress policy on `OnMailerSend`
  (`sandbox.BindMail`).

## Versions

PocketOne has its own version line, starting at `v0.0.1`, independent of PocketBase's numbers. When PocketBase
releases, we merge it and decide then how to bump ours. Each release says which PocketBase version it's based on.

The module path stays `ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase`, so a build pins a PocketOne version through the
`replace` line:

```
replace ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase => github.com/pockethost/pocketone v0.0.1
```

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite

# Multisite

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

Many PocketOne instances behind one listener, routed by hostname. Each request's hostname picks an instance, the
request passes the gates (such as the [firewall](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/firewall)), and a runtime serves it:
[pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker) runs instances in-process, [docker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/docker) runs each in its own container,
and a host can run both. Everything a host plugs in is a host-scope contract: [runtime/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/runtime/v1),
[gate/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/gate/v1), [tls/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/tls/v1),
[http.wrap/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/http.wrap/v1) and [instance.source/v1](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/instance.source/v1).

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Multisite is built into `pocketone`. It takes over `serve` when `pocketone.yaml` has a `multisite` section; without
one, `pocketone serve` runs a single app as usual.

```yaml
multisite: {}
providers:
  runtime/v1: [pocker, docker]   # optional: which runtimes, in preference order (default: every configured one)
```

In your own Go build, pass the host extensions you link (runtimes in preference order), build the host from the
config and run it. [`examples/pocketone/multi.go`](../../examples/pocketone/multi.go) is the stock binary's version:

```go
h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath, Choices: providersSection,
	Extensions: []multisite.Extension{servertiming.New(), autotls.New(), &pocker.Provider{Resolve: cfg.ResolvePath}}})
if errors.Is(err, multisite.ErrNoProvider) {
	// no multisite section in pocketone.yaml: serve a single app instead
}
err = h.Run(ctx)
```

At startup the host logs who provides each host contract, e.g. `multisite: runtime/v1 ← pocker, docker`.

The module is `github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/multisite`.

## Configure

A host reads these `pocketone.yaml` sections:

```yaml
multisite: {}                        # host mode
server:
  https: ":443"                      # the main address
  http: ":80"                        # redirects to https (alone: serves plain HTTP)
  plain: [":8080"]                   # extra plain-HTTP addresses, no redirect (e.g. a private network)
  tls: { cert: cert.pem, key: key.pem }   # reloaded when the files change; or the autotls section
instances:
  file: ./instances.yaml             # where the instances come from
  dev: false                         # also serve unknown hostnames
pocker: { root: ./pb_root }          # a runtime's own section (pocker; docker only runs with its section)
firewall: { allow_cidrs: [10.0.0.0/8] }  # any gate's section turns that gate on
```

- `server` belongs to [Config](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/config); `providers` is the contracts' section. With no `https` or `http`, the host listens on
  `127.0.0.1:8090`.
- The `instances` section is this extension's (keys below). In production the instances file is required; with
  `dev: true` it's optional.
- The `app` section is for a single app and is refused on a multisite host: each instance has its own folder under its
  runtime's root.

### pocketone.yaml reference

#### `instances:`

Where a multi-instance host's instances come from (a YAML file), and dev mode (serve unknown hostnames).

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `file` | string | `instances.yaml` | The instances file (id, hosts and settings for each instance), reloaded when it changes. |
| `dev` | bool |  | Also serve unknown hostnames: each becomes an instance named after it, in dev mode, with its folder made on first use. |

#### `multisite:`

Serve many instances (a multisite host) instead of a single app. The runtimes are the providers of runtime/v1.

## Use

### The instances file

```yaml
instances:
  - id: blog                         # also the folder name: <root>/blog
    hosts: [blog.example.com, www.blog.example.com]
  - id: shop
    hosts: [shop.example.com]
    secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: sk_live_... }               # the app's environment, seen by its JS hooks
    encryption_key: 0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef   # encrypts the app's stored settings
    access: { cors_origins: [https://shop.example.com] }
    limits: { max_js_execution: 60s }                  # over the runtime's defaults
    extensions: { firewall: { trusted_ips: [203.0.113.0/24] } }   # settings for extensions, by name
  - id: old
    hosts: [old.example.com]
    blocked: { status: 402, message: "Payment required" }
```

The file is checked for changes every 2 seconds; edits apply without restarting the host. Ids are lowercase
letters, digits, dots and dashes. Other fields: `version` and `runtime` (which release or runtime runs it), `dir`
(another folder), `dev`, `superusers` (pocker upserts them when the app starts), `private` (for host Go code, never seen by JS) and `remote`
(another server runs it).

### What a request gets

- A hostname no instance maps gets 404, and no folder is created. In dev mode it becomes a new instance named after
  the hostname, in dev mode.
- A `blocked` instance answers every request with its status and message.
- An instance with `remote` set is forwarded there after the gates (a plain proxy to the URL, or
  [Edge](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/edge) for a fleet).
- Contracts the host provides for its instances (docker's remote/v1) answer after the gates and the blocked check,
  so the firewall, rate limits and a powered-off answer apply to them too.
- `GET /.well-known/health` on any hostname reports the host's status, how many instances it knows and how many are
  running.

### Switching runtime

Switching between pocker and docker is a config change (`providers: { runtime/v1: [docker] }`, or an instance's own
`runtime: docker`): both keep instances in `<root>/<id>`. Stop the containers
first when leaving docker (they keep running across a host restart on purpose). Data only moves forward: an instance
started on a newer version than wrote its data is upgraded.

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker) | runtime/v1: every instance runs in this process. |
| [Docker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/docker) | runtime/v1: each instance runs in its own container (with a `docker` section). |
| [Firewall](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/firewall) | A gate: peer allow-list, client IPs and rate limits. On when the config has `firewall` or `rate_limits`. |
| [Edge](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/edge) | Forwards requests for instances another edge runs (the `edges` section). |
| [Mothership](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mothership) | Its mirror is instance.source/v1 instead of the instances file, and lists the other edges. |
| [Auto TLS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/autotls) | Certificates for the main listener, issued for the hostnames instances map. |
| [Stats](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/stats) | Measures disk use and last request for each instance. |
| [Server Timing](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/servertiming) | Server-Timing headers for each step of a request. |

### Building on Host

- **Host extensions.** A `multisite.Extension` (`Name`, `RegisterHost(h)`) provides host-scope contracts on `h.Scope`:
  a runtime (`runtimev1.Contract.ProvideIn(h.Scope, rt)`), a gate, TLS, a wrapper, an instance source. It provides
  nothing when it isn't configured (no section). Pass it in `Options.Extensions`, or `multisite.Link` it from an
  `init` so linking the package is enough (the firewall does). By hand: `h.Use(exts...)`, then `h.Setup(choices)`.
- **Runtime.** `runtimev1.Runtime` (`Name`, `Serves`, `ServeInstance`, `Ready`), with optional `Prechecker`, `Syncer`,
  `Starter`, `Statser` and `Shutdowner`. Each instance runs on the runtime it names, else the first that serves it.
- **Instance source.** `sourcev1.Source` (`Snapshot`, `Watch`) feeds instances from anywhere, such as a control plane.
  The instances file (`YAMLSource`) is the default and steps aside for any other provider.
- **Gates.** A `gatev1.Gate` checks the peer (`AllowPeer`) and admits each request (`Admit`); `ClientIPResolver`
  passes the real client IP on to the app. Gates set on `h.Gates` directly run after the contract's.
- **Forwarding.** `multisite.Options.Forward` serves requests for instances with `remote` set (Edge fills it).
- **Instance routes.** `Host.InstanceRoutes` wrap the runtime for instances this host runs: they run after the
  peer check, the blocked answer and the gates, and before the runtime (never for forwarded instances).
  `multisite.InstanceOf(r)` is the resolved instance and `multisite.InstanceID` fits extkit's host handlers, so a
  contract the host provides for its instances goes here:

  ```go
  remotev1.Contract.ProvideForInstances(h.Scope, myRemote)
  h.InstanceRoutes = append(h.InstanceRoutes, func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
  	return remotev1.W.HostHandler(h.Scope, multisite.InstanceID, myAuth, next)
  })
  ```
- **Listeners and wrappers.** tls/v1 (or `Host.TLS`) sets the listener's TLS, http.wrap/v1 providers wrap the whole
  handler (outside `Host.Wrappers`), and `Host.Background` runs jobs until shutdown.
- **Per-instance settings.** An extension reads its own `extensions.<name>` with `inst.ExtensionConfig(name)` and
  `multisite.DecodeExtensionConfig`.

## Example

A toy host: instances from a YAML file, served by a runtime that answers with the instance it resolved. Run it from
this folder with `go run ./example --instances instances.yaml`, then `curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' localhost:8090/`.

```go
// A minimal host: instances from a YAML file, routed by hostname, served by a toy runtime that answers with the
// instance it resolved. Real hosts plug in a provider instead (ext/pocker in-process, ext/docker in containers).
//
//	go run ./example --instances instances.yaml
//	curl -H 'Host: blog.localhost' localhost:8090/
package main

import (
	"context"
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"net/http"
	"os"
	"os/signal"
	"syscall"

	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/multisite"
)

type echoRuntime struct{}

func (echoRuntime) Name() string                        { return "echo" }
func (echoRuntime) Serves(inst multisite.Instance) bool { return true }
func (echoRuntime) Ready() bool                         { return true }
func (echoRuntime) ServeInstance(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, inst multisite.Instance) {
	fmt.Fprintf(w, "instance %s (%s%s)\n", inst.ID, r.Host, r.URL.Path)
}

func main() {
	instances := flag.String("instances", "instances.yaml", "instances file: instances: [{id: blog, hosts: [blog.localhost]}]")
	listen := flag.String("listen", "127.0.0.1:8090", "listen address")
	flag.Parse()
	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()
	h := &multisite.Host{Source: &multisite.YAMLSource{Path: *instances}, Runtimes: []multisite.Runtime{echoRuntime{}}, Listeners: multisite.Listeners{Listen: *listen}}
	if err := h.Run(ctx); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
```

## How it works

| Piece | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Instance`, `InstanceSource`, `YAMLSource` | The instance record (instance.source/v1) and where instances come from. |
| `Directory` | Instances by hostname and id, kept current from the source. |
| `Handler` | Health path, peer check, hostname, blocked, then remote (the `Forward` hook) or local (the instance routes, then the runtime), with the gates. |
| `Runtime` | runtime/v1: what runs instances. One or more per host, in preference order. |
| `Gate`, `ChainGates`, `HostGate` | Request gates (gate/v1). |
| `Extension`, `Link`, `Host.Use`, `Host.Setup` | Host extensions and the host's contract scope. |
| `Serve`, `TLSProvider` | Listeners: plain, TLS (a provider such as autotls, or cert files reloaded on change), redirect, graceful shutdown. |
| `Host`, `FromConfig` | All of the above assembled, by hand or from `pocketone.yaml`. |
