Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/servertiming

# Server Timing

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

A `Server-Timing` response header on every request to an instance of a [multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite) host: how
long the instance's own handler took, and how long it took to wake the instance for the request (under
[Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker)). Your browser's dev tools show
it in the request's Timing tab.

```
Server-Timing: origin;dur=12.4, wake;dur=0.0
```

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Server Timing is built into `pocketone` and on whenever it serves many instances, whatever the provider. There's
nothing to install. It isn't used for a single app.

In your own host build, list it first among the host extensions, so its header covers every other hop:

```go
h, err := multisite.FromConfig(multisite.Options{Extensions: []multisite.Extension{servertiming.New() /*, other host extensions */}})
```

The module is `github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/servertiming`.

## Configure

There's nothing to configure: no `pocketone.yaml` section, flag or settings screen.

## Use

Open your browser's dev tools, pick a request to an instance and look at its timing, or read the header with curl:

```bash
curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://alpha.localhost:8090/api/health | grep -i server-timing
```

| Entry | What it measures |
|---|---|
| `origin` | The instance's own handler: from handing it the request until it sent its response headers. |
| `wake` | Starting the instance for this request. `0` when it was already running. |

Each value is in milliseconds, one decimal, up to the response headers (time to first byte). The innermost hop comes
first; values a server in front already sent are kept, and this host's entries are added after them.

## Integrations

- **[Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker)** registers `origin` and `wake` for every request it hands to an instance.
- **Add your own entries.** Host code and other extensions call `multisite.Timing(ctx, fn)` during a request; `fn` returns
  `[]multisite.TimingEntry{{Name, Dur, Desc}}` and runs when the headers go out. Only extensions listed after Server Timing
  are covered. Put names in `Desc`, never addresses.
- **Go API.** `FormatTiming`, `AppendServerTiming` and `WithServerTiming` render entries, append them to a header and
  wrap a response writer, for a server that isn't a multisite host.

## Example

There's no `example/main.go`. See it used in [`examples/pocketone/multi.go`](../../examples/pocketone/multi.go), which
lists it first in the `pocketone` binary's host extensions.

## How it works

It's a host wrapper (`multisite.Wrapper`). For each request it starts collecting timing entries in the request's
context, then stamps them into the `Server-Timing` header just before the response headers go out (not on interim
1xx responses). Flush, Hijack and `http.ResponseController` keep working through its writer.

## License

MIT


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/wasm

# WASM

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@octavonu](https://github.com/octavonu)

**Bring your own WASM (BYOW).** Your own code, in Go, Rust, Zig or anything that builds for WASI, in pb_hooks, where
`$os.cmd` and `$os.exec` aren't allowed: a plugin is a small program compiled to WebAssembly that your hooks call like
a function. Input in, output out, or an error. It can't reach the database, files, network, environment or other
processes; your hook gives it what it needs and decides what to do with the result.

```js
// pb_hooks/main.pb.js
onRecordCreate((e) => {
  const out = $wasm.run("summary", { title: e.record.get("title"), body: e.record.get("body") })
  e.record.set("summary", out.text)
  e.next()
}, "posts")
```

Use it for what JS hooks do badly or slowly: parsing (EDIFACT, XML, binary formats), crypto, validation, number
crunching, or a library that only exists in Go, Rust or C.

WASM is an extension; the `.wasm` files it runs are plugins.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

WASM isn't built into `pocketone` yet. In your own build, add it to the [standard set](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/standard),
which every app and every pocker instance gets; the set binds `$wasm` into the JS engine
([`ext/jsvm`](../jsvm/README.md)):

```go
set := standard.New().Add(wasm.New(wasm.Config{})) // $wasm in pb_hooks
```

Without the set, register it and bind it yourself:

```go
p := wasm.New(wasm.Config{})

app := pocketbase.New()
extkit.MustRegister(app, p)
jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{OnInit: func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, p) }})
app.Start()
```

`$wasm` needs PocketOne's JS engine; with PocketBase's own (`--jsvm goja`) extensions bind nothing.

The module is `github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/wasm`. Plugins load from `pb_wasm/`, beside `pb_data/` and
`pb_hooks/`; nothing else needs setting up.

## Configure

The defaults suit most apps. To change them, pass them to `wasm.New`:

| Field | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Dir` | `pb_wasm` beside the data dir | The plugin folder. |
| `MaxCallMemoryMB` | 32 | Memory each call may allocate (its heap, stack and input). Every call has its own, not shared: 8 calls at once may take 8 × 32 MB. A call that needs more crashes alone. |
| `Timeout` | 5s | Time limit for a call's run (compiling comes before it). |
| `MaxConcurrent` | 8 | Calls running at once in the app. More wait, up to `Timeout`, then fail as `busy`. |
| `MaxModulesMB` | 10 | MB of plugin modules running at once: the `.wasm` sizes of the calls running, added up (file sizes, not memory). More wait, as above. It's also the largest module that runs. |
| `MaxPayload` | 4 MB | Largest input or output of a call. |

There's no `pocketone.yaml` section. Under pocker, each instance can override these (see Integrations).

## Use

### Plugins are files

A plugin is `pb_wasm/<name>.wasm`, with an optional `pb_wasm/<name>.json`. The app creates `pb_wasm/` when it
starts, if it isn't there (on a disk it can't write to, it only logs that and serves with no plugins):

```
pb_hooks/main.pb.js
pb_wasm/summary.wasm
pb_wasm/summary.json
```

It ships with the rest of your code: git, `pocketone deploy` (which sends every `pb_*` folder), or SFTP. Like
`node script.js`, every call reads the plugin's files as they are then, so a plugin added, changed or removed takes
effect on the next call, with no restart. To turn a plugin off, remove or rename its `.wasm`. Hidden files and files
that don't end in `.wasm` are ignored, so upload a new version under a hidden name (`.summary.wasm.part`) and rename
it over the old one: no call reads it half written.

A plugin that can't run (a broken module, a bad `.json`, a module over `MaxModulesMB`) fails its calls with
`not_loaded` and says why, and `$wasm.plugins()` says it too; the other plugins run as usual.

`<name>.json` is optional, and so is each of its fields:

```json
{
  "description": "Summarizes a post: its title and first words, and a word count",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "functions": ["run"],
  "language": "Rust",
  "repository": "https://github.com/you/summary",
  "examples": [
    {
      "function": "run",
      "input": {"title": "Hello", "body": "one two three"},
      "output": {"text": "Hello: one two three", "words": 3}
    }
  ]
}
```

| Field | |
|---|---|
| `description` | what it does |
| `version` | the author's version, as you write it (`1.2.0`, `2026-11-15`): up to 32 letters, digits and `.+_-`; only shown |
| `functions` | the functions hooks may call (default `["run"]`) |
| `language` | what it's written in, shown when the module doesn't say: a Go module always does, a Rust one unless it's stripped (`strip = true`), a Zig one never |
| `repository` | where its source is: an `http(s)` URL (no `javascript:`, no credentials), at most 256 characters |
| `examples` | up to 16 calls to try it with: `function` (default `run`), `input` (a JSON string is the plugin's stdin as it is, anything else goes as JSON, as with `$wasm.run`) and, optionally, the `output` it gives |

Nothing runs the examples, reads the version or language, or fetches the repository: they're shown by `$wasm.plugins()`, for people and for tests (run
each example and compare its output). An example works the same locally:
`printf '%s' '{"title":"Hello","body":"one two three"}' | wazero run summary.wasm run`.

Any other field is refused: a plugin can't ask for anything, so a manifest that expects more (dependencies,
permissions) doesn't run without it. A manifest is at most 64 KB.

### Calling from pb_hooks

```js
$wasm.run(name, input)            // the plugin's "run"
$wasm.call(name, function, input) // one of the functions its .json declares
$wasm.plugins()                   // [{name, running, description, version, functions, language, repository, examples,
                                  //   size, error}]
$wasm.limits()                    // {maxCallMemoryMB, timeoutMs, maxConcurrent, maxModulesMB, maxPayload}
$wasm.inspect(name, function, input) // {output, stderr, error, compileMs, runMs}, for trying a plugin out

await $wasm.run.async(name, input) // the same, off the app's JS VM; also $wasm.call.async, $wasm.inspect.async
```

The input is the plugin's stdin: a string or bytes (an `ArrayBuffer`, a `Uint8Array` or another typed array) as they are, nothing for
`undefined` or `null`, anything else as JSON. So `$wasm.run("edifact", e.record.get("raw"))` hands over the raw text,
byte for byte. The output is the plugin's stdout: parsed if it's JSON, a string if not, `null` if empty.

A failed call throws an `Error` named `WasmError`, with `code`, `message`, `retryable` and `plugin`:

```js
try {
  e.record.set("summary", $wasm.run("summary", post).text)
} catch (err) {
  if (err.name !== "WasmError" || err.code !== "empty_body") throw err
}
```

| Code | |
|---|---|
| `not_found` | no `<name>.wasm` in the folder |
| `not_loaded` | in the folder, but it can't run (the message says why: a broken module, a bad `.json`, too large), or the app isn't serving |
| `no_such_function` | the function isn't in its `.json` |
| `timeout` | over the time limit (retryable) |
| `crashed` | it trapped, panicked or ran out of memory |
| `too_large` | input or output over the limit |
| `busy` | the calls running left no room for this one (retryable); the message gives the numbers |
| `plugin_error` | it exited non-zero without a code of its own |
| anything else | the plugin's own code (below) |

`$wasm.inspect` makes the same call but never throws for it: it returns the output (or `null`), the `error` as
`{code, message, retryable}` (or `null`), what the plugin wrote to stderr (up to 64 KB), and how long compiling and
running took. It's for pages that let a superuser try a plugin out; hooks use `run` and `call`.

The JS engine runs one VM per app, and `run` and `call` hold it while the plugin compiles and runs: the app's
other hooks and requests wait. That's fine for a plugin that answers in milliseconds (Rust, Zig). For a slow one (a
Go plugin compiles for over a second each call) or many calls at once, use `.async` in an async hook, so the app
serves other requests meanwhile:

```js
onRecordCreate(async (e) => {
  const out = await $wasm.run.async("summary", { title: e.record.get("title"), body: e.record.get("body") })
  e.record.set("summary", out.text)
  return e.next()
}, "posts")
```

The time limit covers the run; compiling comes before it (below).

`$wasm` is declared in each app's `pb_data/types.d.ts` ([`wasm.d.ts`](wasm.d.ts)), for code completion and `tsc`.

### Writing a plugin

A plugin is a plain WASI program (`wasip1`), the way you'd write a command-line tool: read stdin, write stdout, exit.
The function asked for is its first argument (`os.Args[1]`, `"run"` for `$wasm.run`). To fail, exit non-zero; if
stderr is a JSON object `{"code", "message", "retryable"}`, hooks get it as is, any other text becomes the
`message` of a `plugin_error`. Anything it writes to stderr on success goes to the app's log (Logs in the
dashboard), so stderr is its log.

**Go** ([`example/summary`](example/summary/main.go)):

```go
func main() {
	var post struct{ Title, Body string }
	if err := json.NewDecoder(os.Stdin).Decode(&post); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprint(os.Stderr, `{"code":"bad_input","message":"not a post"}`)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
	json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(map[string]any{"text": post.Title, "words": len(strings.Fields(post.Body))})
}
```

```sh
GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o pb_wasm/summary.wasm .
```

**Rust** ([`example/summary-rust`](example/summary-rust/src/main.rs)): a binary crate, serde for JSON.

```sh
rustup target add wasm32-wasip1   # once
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1
```

**Zig** ([`example/summary-zig`](example/summary-zig/src/main.zig)): an executable for `wasm32-wasi`. Set
`stack_size = 1 << 20` in `build.zig`: Zig's default stack is 16 MB, and every call would start with it.

Any language that builds a WASI program works the same way (C, TinyGo, AssemblyScript with WASI, ...). Try a
plugin without an app: `echo '{"title":"Hi","body":"one two"}' | wazero run summary.wasm run`.

Two things are refused when the plugin loads, with a message that says so:

- a library instead of a program: Go's `-buildmode=c-shared`, or any module without `_start` ("not a WASI program");
- a module that imports anything outside `wasi_snapshot_preview1`, such as an [Extism](https://extism.org) plugin
  built with its PDK, or host functions this host doesn't have.

### Which language

| Example plugin | Module | Checked when its file loads | Per call | Memory per call: compiled code + the program's own |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Go | 4.4 MB | 240 ms | 1.7 s | ~20–30 MB + 3.6 MB |
| Rust | 95 KB | 37 ms | 39 ms | ~2–5 MB + 1.1 MB |
| Zig | 55 KB | 39 ms | 23 ms | ~2.5 MB + 1.2 MB |

Every call compiles the plugin from scratch and runs it, and nothing compiled is kept: a plugin takes memory only
while a call runs, however many plugins the apps have: between calls, nothing. The compiled
code is most of it; the program's own memory (its stack and heap, Go's runtime and garbage collector included) stays
under `MaxCallMemoryMB`. Compiling is almost all of a call's time: the summary itself runs in a few milliseconds. Measured on
a laptop (2026-11-14), one call at a time; the compiled code's size is approximate, and a Go plugin's varies with
what it imports (one that imports `net/http` is ~11 MB).

Go calls compiling at once also slow each other down: one took +19 MB, two +38 MB, four +245 MB (2026-11-16). That's
why the calls running at once are limited by their modules' size, `MaxModulesMB`, and not only by their number. An
admin picks the trade-off with that one number:

| `MaxModulesMB` | Go calls (4.4 MB) at once | Rust or Zig calls (~0.1 MB) | Most memory they take, measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 1 | 8 (`MaxConcurrent`) | ~25 MB |
| 10 (default) | 2 | 8 | ~45 MB |
| 20 | 4 | 8 | ~250 MB |

Pick by what the plugin does. Go is the easiest to write and fine where a call can take a second or two (a cron job,
an import, an admin action). A plugin on a hot path (every record save, every request) is better in Rust or Zig,
whose calls are 40 times faster and take a seventh of the memory.

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker) | One extension value serves every instance (the standard set). Each instance has its own plugins, in its own `pb_wasm/`, its own call slots and limits. Each call reads the instance's `pb_wasm/` as it is then; nothing runs between calls (below). |
| [Sandbox](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/sandbox) | `$wasm` is safe to give a hostile tenant: a plugin gets nothing but its input. A call can't be interrupted by the JS engine's time limits, so `Timeout` (and compiling) bound it instead. |
| [Deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy) | `pocketone deploy` sends `pb_wasm/` with the other `pb_*` folders; the next call of each plugin runs the new version, with no restart. |

### Per-instance settings (pocker)

Each instance can override `maxCallMemoryMB`, `maxConcurrent`, `maxModulesMB`, `timeout` (a duration, like `5s`) and
`maxPayload` in its `extensions.wasm` settings, over the Config given to `New`, key by key. `enabled: false` turns
`$wasm` off for that instance (`typeof $wasm === "undefined"` in its hooks). A change restarts just that instance, on
its next request:

```yaml
instances:
  - id: abc
    extensions: { wasm: { timeout: 10s, maxCallMemoryMB: 64 } }
  - id: no-plugins
    extensions: { wasm: { enabled: false } }
```

Leave `dir` unset there: each instance then gets the `pb_wasm/` in its own folder. `MaxConcurrent` and
`MaxModulesMB` count per instance, so one instance's busy plugins never make another's calls wait. A restart (new
settings, a pb_hooks change, a restore) lets calls in progress finish, and the instance's plugins run as before
after it, from its folder: nothing to reload.

### Building on WASM

There's no Go API, endpoint or form for calling a plugin: pb_hooks (`$wasm`) are the only way in, so whatever
reaches a plugin went through the app's own code.

## Example

[`example/main.go`](example/main.go) runs one app with a `posts` collection and the hook above; its folder is laid
out like an instance (`pb_data/`, `pb_hooks/`, `pb_wasm/`). Build the plugin into `example/pb_wasm/`, then
`cd example && go run . serve --dev` and create a post.

```go
// Command example runs one app with ext/wasm and the summary plugin wired in from pb_hooks: a new post gets its
// summary before it's saved (pb_hooks/main.pb.js). The example folder is the app's folder, laid out like an
// instance on PocketHost: pb_data/, pb_hooks/ and pb_wasm/ side by side.
//
//	cd example && go run . serve --dev
//
// Build the plugin into pb_wasm/ (before or after starting the app: each call reads it):
//
//	mkdir -p pb_wasm && cp summary/plugin.json pb_wasm/summary.json
//	(cd summary && GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build -o ../pb_wasm/summary.wasm .)
//
// Then create a post (dashboard, or the API) and look at its summary field.
//
// Logins (ext/devusers, local testing only): dashboard admin@example.com / password, app user user@example.com / password.
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase/core"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/extkit"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/extkit/js"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/wasm"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app) // local testing: superuser admin@example.com and user user@example.com, password "password"
	app.OnBootstrap().BindFunc(func(e *core.BootstrapEvent) error {
		if err := e.Next(); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		return posts(e.App)
	})
	// the same extension value the standard set gives every pocker instance (set.Add(wasm.New(...)))
	plugins := wasm.New(wasm.Config{})
	extkit.MustRegister(app, plugins)
	jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{
		HooksDir: "pb_hooks",
		OnInit:   func(rt js.Runtime) { extkit.BindJS(app, rt, plugins) }, // $wasm in pb_hooks
	})
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

func posts(app core.App) error {
	if _, err := app.FindCollectionByNameOrId("posts"); err == nil {
		return nil
	}
	c := core.NewBaseCollection("posts")
	c.Fields.Add(&core.TextField{Name: "title"}, &core.TextField{Name: "body", Max: 100000},
		&core.TextField{Name: "summary", Max: 1000}, &core.NumberField{Name: "words"})
	return app.Save(c)
}
```

### More example plugins

Each is a plain program with a `plugin.json` (its functions and examples, so `/wasm`-style pages and the wazero CLI
can try it), built with the command in its header. They answer the usual questions about a feature like this:

| Plugin | Language | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| [`summary`](example/summary), [`summary-rust`](example/summary-rust), [`summary-zig`](example/summary-zig) | Go, Rust, Zig | The same plugin in three languages: the hook above, and how much the language matters (a Go module is ~4 MB and compiles for over a second; Rust and Zig, under 100 KB and ~40 ms). |
| [`crypto`](example/crypto) | Go | What an app used to run with `$os.exec`: AES-256-GCM. The key comes in with each call; the plugin can't keep it or send it anywhere. |
| [`waflows`](example/waflows) | Rust | What pb_hooks can't do: a WhatsApp Flows endpoint needs RSA-OAEP and AES-GCM with WhatsApp's key and IV. The hook keeps the JSON and HTTP; the plugin does only those two. |
| [`edifact-orders-rust`](example/edifact-orders-rust) | Rust | A real format with a real library (edifact-rs): an EDIFACT ORDERS message, as raw text, read into an order. |
| [`order-xml`](example/order-xml) | Rust | The same order from XML (roxmltree), so a hook takes either format and stores one shape. |
| [`devil`](example/devil) | Rust | Is it safe? It tries, in plain sight, to read the app's database and `/etc/passwd`, list folders, write a file, read the environment, run `sh -c id` and send to `attacker.example`. Every try says `refused`. |
| [`memhog`](example/memhog) | Rust | What does it cost? It asks for more memory than `MaxCallMemoryMB`: that call fails as `crashed`, saying which limit it hit, and the app goes on. `probe` shows the limit from inside. |

## What a plugin can't do

Plugins run in [wazero](https://wazero.io) (pure Go, no cgo), in the app's process, with only the standard WASI
functions and nothing behind them:

- **No files:** nothing is mounted, not even `pb_wasm/`. `open` fails.
- **No network:** WASI preview 1 has no way to connect. (Go's `net` on wasip1 is an in-memory stand-in: a plugin can
  "listen", but nothing outside the program reaches it.)
- **No environment, no processes**, no arguments beyond the function name.
- **No state between calls:** every call gets a fresh instance, so nothing from one call (or one caller) reaches the
  next.
- **Bounded:** memory, time, input and output size, and how many calls run at once (see Configure).

It does get a real clock and real random numbers (crypto nonces need them). Data from the app, secrets and API
responses reach a plugin only as input from your hook, and the result goes nowhere but back to the hook: the network
stays with `$http.send` in pb_hooks.

## How it works

- Plugins run only while the app serves (other commands, such as `migrate`, never read them, nor create the
  folder).
- Like `node script.js`: each call reads its plugin's files (`<name>.json`, then `<name>.wasm` once the call has
  room), compiles the module in a wazero runtime of its own, runs it, and closes it after. Nothing stays in memory
  between calls, so a folder of 100 plugins costs nothing while they aren't called, and no compilation cache, in
  memory or on disk. Compiling validates the module: a broken or half-written one doesn't run. A call in progress
  finishes with what it read, whatever happens to the file meanwhile. Compiling counts toward `MaxConcurrent` and
  `MaxModulesMB`, so the memory it takes stays bounded too.
- Nothing watches the folder: no inotify watches (Linux allows only 128 per user by default, and pocker runs many
  apps in one process), no timer, no work between calls, however many instances there are.
- `$wasm.plugins()` lists the folder each time. It checks each module with wazero's interpreter, which validates it
  without making machine code (~180 ms for a Go plugin), and keeps only what it found (manifest, language, error)
  until the plugin's files change size or time; when the app starts serving, it checks them all once, so the log says
  which ones can't run.
- A call waits for room: fewer than `MaxConcurrent` calls running, and its module's size left in `MaxModulesMB`
  (`$wasm.plugins()` gives each one's `size`). Compiling takes time and memory in step with a module's size, so with
  the defaults (8 calls, 10 MB) a Rust or Zig plugin (~0.1 MB) runs 8 calls at once and a Go one (~4.4 MB) 2, beside
  small ones. A call goes in as soon as there's room for it, so a small call doesn't queue behind a big one that's
  waiting; under a steady stream of small calls, a big one may wait until it gives up as `busy`.
- No collection and no database use: what's in the folder, and why a plugin can't run, comes from the files
  (`$wasm.plugins()` and the log).

# Multitenant

Version 0.0.0 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

Accounts that own instances, for hosting other people (level 4): each instance has an owner; accounts have quotas and
can be suspended; owners log in to their instances' dashboards (their login is kept in sync as a superuser); owners
get API tokens for the CLI and deploys; and an API your own tenant dashboard talks to (PocketHost's dashboard is one).

**Runs on:** [mothership](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mothership) (level 3) and [pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker); requires the
[sandbox](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/sandbox), since tenants run code you don't control.

> **Planned.** Nothing is published here yet. See [Create your own extension](https://pocketone.dev/docs/writing-an-extension).

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Not available yet: Multitenant isn't in `pocketone` and has no Go module to add to a custom build.

## Configure

Nothing to configure yet. Its settings will be documented here when it ships.

## Use

Nothing to use yet. It is planned to give each instance an owner account, with quotas, suspension, dashboard sign-in for owners and API tokens for the CLI and deploys.

## Integrations

It is planned to work with these extensions:

- **Mothership:** adds an `owner` to instances and an accounts table through the mothership's schema hooks, and adds
  owner-derived values (superusers, blocked status, extension settings) to what edges receive through its feed hooks.
- **Settings for other extensions:** written into each instance's `extensions:` block, e.g. an owner's trusted IPs for the
  [firewall](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/firewall) or a plan's retention for [pitr](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr). Those extensions don't know
  tenants exist.
- **Deploy:** supplies the tenant-token backend for the [deploy](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/deploy) API.
- **Billing:** a billing provider hook; [tenant-billing-ls](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/tenant-billing-ls) is the Lemon Squeezy one.

## Example

No example yet; it will come with the extension.

# Multitenant Billing

Version 0.0.0 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

provider hook that adapters implement (checkout links, webhooks, renewals, cancellations, refunds), applying a
subscription's plan to an account, and a reconcile job that compares accounts with the provider.

**Runs on:** [tenants](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/tenants) (level 4). Providers are separate extensions, e.g.

# Lemon Squeezy Adapter

# Standard Set

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

The extensions every PocketOne app has: settings, API tokens (with the OAuth server), remotes (remote/v1), MCP,
PocketPages, S3 redirects, point-in-time restore, backups, bulk mail and deploy. The stock `pocketone` binary and every Pocker instance use it,
so an app never misses one because its host forgot to list it. Members can be reconfigured or turned off per app,
never removed.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

The standard set is built into `pocketone`. In your own Go build, make the app with it instead of
`pocketbase.New()`:

```go
set := standard.New()
app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks"})
app.Start()
```

`NewApp` registers the members, loads `pb_hooks` with their JS APIs (`$mcp`, `$tokens`, `$bulkmail`) and resolves
their contracts. On an app you built yourself, call `set.Register(app, jsvmConfig)` instead.

## Configure

- **Reconfigure a member:** replace it, e.g. `set.PITR = pitr.New(pitr.Config{Retention: 7 * 24 * time.Hour})`. A
  member set to nil is an error.
- **Turn one off:** `enabled: false` in its `pocketone.yaml` section, or in an instance's `extensions.<name>` under
  Pocker. Extensions that require it turn off too, and say why.
- **Add your own:** `set.Add(myextension.New())`. Extras register after the members, under the same rules.
- **Pick providers:** `set.Providers` is `pocketone.yaml`'s `providers:` section, for a contract more than one
  extension provides.

### pocketone.yaml reference

#### `providers:`

Which extension provides a contract when several do.

## Use

Each app logs what it got when it starts:

```
standard: on: settings, tokens, remotes, mcp, pages, s3redirect, pitr, backups, bulkmail, deploy
standard: tokens/v1 ← tokens
```

With remotes off (deploy requires its remote/v1):

```
standard: remotes off: enabled: false
standard: deploy off: needs remote/v1, which nothing provides
```

## Integrations

| With | What happens |
|---|---|
| [Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker) | Every instance gets the set (`Server.Standard`), with its own `extensions.<name>` settings. |
| [Contracts](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/all) | Members find each other through contracts (`tokens/v1`), resolved per app; the startup lines show who provides what. |

## Example

```go
// A PocketOne app with the standard set and one extra extension: run it with `go run . serve`.
package main

import (
	"log"
	"time"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/pitr"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/standard"
)

func main() {
	set := standard.New()
	set.PITR = pitr.New(pitr.Config{Retention: 7 * 24 * time.Hour}) // reconfigure a member
	set.Add(mailtrap.New())                                         // add your own

	app := set.NewApp(pocketbase.Config{}, jsvm.Config{HooksDir: "pb_hooks"})
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## License

MIT


---

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mailtrap

# Mail Trap

Version 0.0.1 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

A development mail catcher (like MailDev or Mailpit) for testing an extension or app that sends mail. In dev mode, an
app whose SMTP is off sends its mail here instead of the host's `sendmail`, and you read it at http://127.0.0.1:8025.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Mail Trap is built into `pocketone`, for a single app and for every pocker instance on a multisite host. There's
nothing to install: run `pocketone serve --dev` with SMTP off and it's active.

In your own Go build, register it before the app starts:

```go
app := pocketbase.New()
mailtrap.MustRegister(app)
app.Start()
```

Under Pocker, add `mailtrap.New()` to the extensions. The module is `github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap`.

## Configure

There is no `pocketone.yaml` section or settings screen. It turns itself on only when both are true:

- the app is in dev mode (`serve --dev`, or a dev instance under Pocker), and
- the app's SMTP is off (Settings → Mail).

Turn SMTP on, or run without `--dev`, and it does nothing. Two environment variables move its ports:

| Variable | Default |
|---|---|
| `P1_MAILTRAP_HTTP` | `127.0.0.1:8025` (the web inbox) |
| `P1_MAILTRAP_SMTP` | `127.0.0.1:1025` (SMTP) |

Never expose these ports: anyone who can reach them can read the mail.

## Use

1. Start the app with `--dev`. It prints the inbox address once it's active.
2. Make your extension or app send mail: a verification, a password reset, `$app.newMailClient()`, a bulk mail campaign.
   Each caught message is also printed as one line in the terminal.
3. Open http://127.0.0.1:8025. The list refreshes every 2 seconds. Click a message to see it as **HTML**, **Text** or
   **Raw** source. **Clear** empties the inbox.

It keeps the last 500 messages, in memory only; they're gone when the process exits. If its ports are taken, it still
catches mail and prints each message in the terminal.

## Integrations

### Works with

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [Contracts](https://pocketone.dev/docs/contracts/all) | Provides `mail.fallback/v1`: with SMTP off, an app's mail goes to the contract's providers in order (`providers: { mail.fallback/v1: [mailtrap, mailrelay] }`); in dev mode Mail Trap takes it, otherwise it passes it on. |
| [Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker) | One inbox for every dev instance. Each message is labeled with the instance that sent it (its `X-Pocker-Instance` header), and the inbox filters by instance. |
| [Mail Relay](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mailrelay) | Mail Relay's example uses the trap's SMTP port as its relay, so relayed mail goes through the real SMTP path and lands here. |
| [Bulk Mail](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bulkmail) | In dev mode with SMTP off, campaign mail lands in the inbox instead of being sent. |

### Building on Mail Trap

- **Its hook runs last.** It binds `OnMailerSend` after the app's own hooks, so your `onMailerSend` hooks still run
  and can change the message first. When it takes a message it never calls the next handler, so `sendmail` never runs.
- **SMTP for other tools.** The SMTP listener accepts any message (and any AUTH), so anything that speaks SMTP can
  send to it.
- **Go API.** `mailtrap.Default(reason)` returns the process-wide trap, starting it on first use. A `Trap` has
  `Messages()`, `Clear()`, `Add(from, to, raw, label)` and `AddMessage(msg, label)`, and `Handler()` serves the inbox.
  `Trap{SMTPAddr, HTTPAddr}.Start(ctx)` runs a separate trap, for example in a test.
- **Inbox API.** `GET /api/messages` (newest first, without bodies), `GET /api/messages/{id}`,
  `GET /api/messages/{id}/raw` (.eml) and `DELETE /api/messages`, on the inbox address.

## Example

[`example/main.go`](example/main.go) runs one app in dev mode with the trap. Run `go run ./example serve --dev` from
this folder, request a password reset for `user@example.com` (password `password`) from the dashboard (log in as
`admin@example.com` / `password`), and read the mail at http://127.0.0.1:8025.

```go
// Command example runs one app in dev mode with the dev mail trap: request a password reset for user@example.com
// in the dashboard and read the mail at http://127.0.0.1:8025.
//
//	go run ./example serve --dev
package main

import (
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/mailtrap"
)

func main() {
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app)
	mailtrap.MustRegister(app)
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## How it works

It's built on PocketBase's own `OnMailerSend` hook (the same way [Mail Relay](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mailrelay) takes over an
instance's mail), so PocketBase is unchanged. It used to live in core (`tools/mailer/trap.go`); it moved here on
2026-11-13.

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/bundle

# Bundle

Version 0.1.0 · Owners: [@benallfree](https://github.com/benallfree)

Ship an app's files inside the binary instead of folders on disk: its JS hooks (`pb_hooks`), migrations
(`pb_migrations`) and public files (`pb_public`). Nothing is written to disk and nothing on disk can override them.
PocketHost's mothership uses it for its own hooks. Formerly `jsembed`.

[Install](#install) · [Configure](#configure) · [Use](#use) · [Integrations](#integrations) · [Example](#example)

## Install

Bundle is not in the `pocketone` binary. Add it to your own Go build: embed the folders, pass the hooks and migrations
to [jsvm](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm) as extensions, and serve the public files.

```go
//go:embed hooks migrations public
var files embed.FS

hooks, _ := fs.Sub(files, "hooks")
migrations, _ := fs.Sub(files, "migrations")
public, _ := fs.Sub(files, "public")
jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{
	Extensions: []any{bundle.Hooks(hooks), bundle.Migrations(migrations)},
})
bundle.Public(app, public, true)
```

The module is `github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/bundle`.

## Configure

Nothing to configure. List only what you bundle: without `bundle.Hooks`, hooks still come from `HooksDir` on disk,
and the same for migrations.

## Use

- **Hooks:** `.pb.js` files come from the FS's root only. `HooksDir` is ignored, nothing is written to it, and hooks
  aren't watched.
- **Migrations:** files come from the FS's root only; `MigrationsDir` is ignored.
- **`require()`:** `__hooks` is the virtual root `/pb_embedded/pb_hooks`. Paths under it, and relative paths, load
  from the hooks FS. Everything else is "module not found": absolute disk paths, `..` escapes, `node_modules`. JS that
  reads files itself (`$os.readFile(__hooks + ...)`) gets "no such file", since the root doesn't exist on disk.
- **Public files:** `bundle.Public(app, fsys, indexFallback)` serves the FS at `GET /{path...}` like `pb_public`,
  unless the app has its own route there. With `indexFallback`, unknown paths serve `index.html` (single-page apps).

## Integrations

| Extension | How they fit |
|---|---|
| [JSVM](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/jsvm) | `Hooks` and `Migrations` are jsvm extensions (`HookFiles`, `Modules`, `MigrationFiles`). |

## Example

```go
// Command example serves its JS hooks and public files from files embedded in the binary: no pb_hooks or pb_public
// folder on disk.
//
//	go run ./example serve
//	curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/hello
//	curl http://127.0.0.1:8090/
package main

import (
	"embed"
	"io/fs"
	"log"

	"ganigeorgiev.com/pocketbase/pocketbase"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/bundle"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/devusers"
	"github.com/pockethost/pocketone/ext/jsvm"
)

//go:embed hooks public
var files embed.FS

func main() {
	hooks, err := fs.Sub(files, "hooks")
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	public, err := fs.Sub(files, "public")
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	app := pocketbase.New()
	devusers.Register(app)
	jsvm.MustRegister(app, jsvm.Config{Extensions: []any{bundle.Hooks(hooks)}})
	bundle.Public(app, public, true)
	if err := app.Start(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## How it works

`Hooks` implements jsvm's `HookFiles` and `Modules`: the engine asks it for the hook files and for every module
`require()` resolves, and it serves only paths under the virtual root, from the FS. `Migrations` implements
`MigrationFiles`. `Public` binds the static route with `apis.Static` at the lowest priority, as PocketBase does for
`pb_public`.

## License

MIT

Source: https://pocketone.dev/docs/config-reference

# pocketone.yaml reference

Every section the `pocketone` binary understands, from `pocketone config --json`. Each extension owns its own section. `pocketone config check` checks a file. How the file works (where it's found, `.env` secrets) is on the [Config](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/config) page.

#### `app:`

The single app: data dir, dev mode, encryption, hooks, migrations, public dir, and the .env names it may read (env_allow). Not used on a multisite host.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dir` | string |  | The data folder (pb_data). Default: pb_data next to the executable. The --dir flag wins. |
| `dev` | bool |  | Dev mode: logs and SQL statements printed to the console. The --dev flag wins. |
| `encryption_env` | string |  | Name of the environment variable holding a 32-character key that encrypts the app settings. The --encryptionEnv flag wins. |
| `query_timeout` | duration |  | Default timeout for SELECT queries, such as 30s. The --queryTimeout flag wins. |
| `hooks_dir` | string |  | The JS hooks folder. Default: pb_hooks next to pb_data. The --hooksDir flag wins. |
| `hooks_watch` | bool |  | Restart the app when a pb_hooks file changes. On unless false. The --hooksWatch flag wins. |
| `jsvm` | string |  | The JS engine for pb_hooks and pb_migrations: quickjs (PocketOne's, the default) or goja (PocketBase's own, for pure PocketBase compatibility: pages, $mcp, $tokens and JS contracts are off). The --jsvm flag wins. |
| `hooks_pool` | int |  | Only with jsvm: goja: how many JS runtimes are kept ready for hooks. Default 15. The --hooksPool flag wins. |
| `migrations_dir` | string |  | The migrations folder. Default: pb_migrations next to pb_data. The --migrationsDir flag wins. |
| `automigrate` | bool |  | Write a migration file when you change collections in the dashboard. On unless false. The --automigrate flag wins. |
| `public_dir` | string |  | The static files folder. Default: pb_public next to the executable. The --publicDir flag wins. |
| `index_fallback` | bool |  | Serve index.html for a missing static path, for single-page apps. On unless false. The --indexFallback flag wins. |
| `env_allow` | list of string |  | Names from the .env the app and its JS hooks may read. Default none. |

#### `autotls:`

Automatic HTTPS certificates (ACME): auto, email, CA, domains, DNS-01, certificate storage. The --autotls* flags win.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `auto` | bool |  | Get certificates through ACME (CertMagic). Flag: --autotls. |
| `email` | string |  | ACME account email, for expiry notices from the CA. Flag: --autotlsEmail. |
| `ca` | string |  | letsencrypt (default), letsencrypt-staging, zerossl, or an ACME directory URL. Flag: --autotlsCA. |
| `storage` | string |  | Where certificates are kept. Default pb_data/.autotls. |
| `domains` | list of string |  | Extra domains to get at start; wildcards (*.example.com) need dns. Flag: --autotlsDomains. |
| `dns.provider` | string |  | DNS provider for DNS-01 challenges (needed for wildcards): cloudflare. Flag: --autotlsDNS. |
| `dns.api_token` | string |  | The provider's API token. Write $VAR to read it from the .env beside the file. |
| `dns.api_token_env` | string |  | Or: the environment variable holding the token. Default CF_API_TOKEN. Flag: --autotlsDNSTokenEnv. |

Owned by [Auto TLS](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/autotls).

#### `docker:`

Runtime provider docker: each instance in its own container with the PocketBase (pb:) or PocketOne (p1:) binary of its version (image, binary cache and manifest, instance root, default version, idle stop, limits).

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `socket` | string |  | The Docker socket. Default $DOCKER_HOST when it is unix://, else /var/run/docker.sock. |
| `image` | string |  | Base image the binaries run in, such as alpine:3.20. Required; pulled when missing. |
| `binaries` | string |  | Folder of the release binary cache and its releases.json. Required. |
| `versions` | list of string |  | The minors this host serves, such as pb:0.36 or p1:0.0 (latest patch of each, from docker update). |
| `root` | string |  | Folder with one folder per instance (<root>/<id>). Required. |
| `home` | string |  | The instance folder inside the container. Default /home/pockethost. |
| `default_version` | string |  | Version for instances that name none, such as p1:0.0.*. Empty: such instances fail. |
| `min_upstream` | string |  | Oldest upstream PocketBase release served. Default 0.23.0; lower it only for releases you cache yourself. |
| `idle_ttl` | duration |  | Stop a container after this long without requests. Default 10m. |
| `max_concurrent_starts` | int |  | Containers starting at once. Default 4. |
| `start_timeout` | duration |  | How long a container gets to answer its health check. Default 60s. |
| `nano_cpus` | int |  | CPU limit per container in billionths of a CPU (1000000000 = one CPU). 0: no limit. |
| `pids_limit` | int |  | Process limit per container. 0: Docker's default. |
| `nofile` | list of int |  | Open-file limit per container: [soft, hard]. Empty: Docker's default. |
| `cap_drop` | list of string |  | Linux capabilities to drop, such as [ALL]. |
| `no_new_privileges` | bool |  | Set no-new-privileges on every container. |
| `network` | string |  | Docker network for the containers. Default the bridge. |
| `adopt_image` | string |  | Also adopt running unlabeled containers of this image named after an instance id (taking over from another manager). |

Owned by [Docker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/docker).

#### `edges:`

The fleet: this edge's id and a fixed list of the other edges (id, internal_url, region).

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `self` | string |  | This edge's id, such as lax-1. |
| `list` | list of object |  | The other edges: id, internal_url (where this edge reaches it) and optional region. |

Owned by [Edge](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/edge).

#### `firewall:`

Peers allowed to connect, trusted proxies and client-IP headers, trusted clients, the rate-limit header prefix. Turns the firewall on.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `allow_cidrs` | list of string |  | Peers (IPs or CIDRs) allowed to connect; others get 403. Empty: everyone. |
| `trusted_proxies` | list of string |  | Peers whose client-IP headers are believed. |
| `client_ip_headers` | list of string |  | Headers read, in order, for the client IP from a trusted proxy. Default CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP. |
| `trusted_clients` | list of string |  | Client IPs or CIDRs that get the trusted rate limits on every instance. |
| `trusted_client_headers` | list of string |  | Headers a trusted client uses to name its end user's IP, so each user gets their own limits. Default X-Client-IP. |
| `rate_limit_header_prefix` | string |  | Prefix of the rate-limit response headers. Default X-RateLimit. |

Owned by [Firewall](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/firewall).

#### `instances:`

Where a multi-instance host's instances come from (a YAML file), and dev mode (serve unknown hostnames).

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `file` | string | `instances.yaml` | The instances file (id, hosts and settings for each instance), reloaded when it changes. |
| `dev` | bool |  | Also serve unknown hostnames: each becomes an instance named after it, in dev mode, with its folder made on first use. |

Owned by [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite).

#### `lifecycle:`

Instance data on this host: how often disk use is measured and last-request times are reported.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `measure_every` | duration | `24h0m0s` | How old an instance's disk measurement may get before it is measured again. Default 24h. |
| `report_every` | duration | `1h0m0s` | How often changed last-request times are reported to the sink. Default 1h. |
| `concurrency` | int | `2` | How many instances are measured at once. Default 2. |

Owned by [Stats](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/stats).

#### `mothership:`

A community mothership to mirror instances and edges from: url, login, this edge's id, internal URL, region, apex.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `url` | string |  | The mothership's URL. Required. |
| `email` | string |  | Superuser email this edge logs in with; use a $VAR from the .env. |
| `password` | string |  | Superuser password; use a $VAR from the .env. |
| `self` | string |  | This edge's edge_id, such as lax-1. Default: the edges section's self. Required. |
| `internal_url` | string |  | Where other edges reach this one. Set: the edge registers itself when the mothership has no record for it. |
| `region` | string |  | Region recorded when the edge registers itself. |
| `apex` | string |  | Makes <name>.<apex> a hostname of every instance. Empty: hosts only. |
| `heartbeat` | duration |  | How often this edge marks itself online. Default 15s; negative: never. |
| `resync` | duration |  | How often everything is reloaded, in case a change was missed. Default 10m. |

Owned by [Mothership](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/mothership).

#### `multisite:`

Serve many instances (a multisite host) instead of a single app. The runtimes are the providers of runtime/v1.

Owned by [Multisite](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/multisite).

#### `pitr:`

Point-in-time restore: on by default, retention, snapshot interval. The --pitr and --pitrRetention flags win.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | bool |  | On unless false. The --pitr flag wins. |
| `retention` | duration |  | How far back a restore can go. Default 72h. The --pitrRetention flag wins. |
| `snapshot_interval` | duration |  | How often a full copy is taken. Default 24h. Shorter: faster restores, more storage. |

Owned by [PITR](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pitr).

#### `pocker:`

Runtime provider pocker: instances run in-process (root folder, hooks pool, egress allow list, instance limit defaults).

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `root` | string | `./pb_root` | The folder holding one folder per instance: <root>/<id>. |
| `hooks_pool_size` | int | `2` | Ignored: each instance has one JS VM (ext/jsvm). Kept so existing configs load. |
| `max_js_execution` | duration | `30s` | Longest any single JS call (hook, route, cron job, migration) may run. |
| `max_js_allocation` | int | `67108864` | Largest result a JS built-in may allocate in one step, such as 64MiB. |
| `max_call_stack_size` | int | `2000` | Deepest JS recursion allowed. |
| `max_sleep` | duration | `10s` | Longest a JS sleep() call may wait. |
| `max_query_duration` | duration | `30s` | Longest an SQL statement without its own deadline may run. |
| `http_send_max_timeout` | duration | `1m0s` | Longest timeout a JS $http.send call may use. |
| `http_send_max_body` | int | `10485760` | Largest response body a JS $http.send call may read, such as 10MiB. |
| `max_concurrent_js` | int | `16` | JS calls an instance runs at once; more wait up to max_js_execution, then fail. |
| `egress_allow` | list of string |  | Private networks (CIDRs) instances may still connect to. Default none: public addresses only. |

Owned by [Pocker](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/pocker).

#### `providers:`

Which extension provides a contract when several do.

Owned by [Standard Set](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/standard).

#### `rate_limits:`

Default rate limits for every instance (per instance: extensions.firewall.rate_limits). Turns the firewall on.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ip_hourly` | int |  | Requests per hour from one client IP to one instance. Default 1000. |
| `instance_hourly` | int |  | Requests per hour to one instance from everyone. Default 10000. |
| `ip_concurrent` | int |  | Requests one client IP may have open on one instance at once. Default 15. |
| `instance_concurrent` | int |  | Requests one instance may have open at once. Default 250. |
| `file_weight` | number |  | What a /api/files request costs, as a share of a request. Default 0.1. |
| `trusted.ip_hourly` | int |  | Requests per hour from one trusted client IP to one instance. |
| `trusted.instance_hourly` | int |  | Requests per hour to one instance. |
| `trusted.ip_concurrent` | int |  | Requests one trusted client IP may have open on one instance at once. |
| `trusted.instance_concurrent` | int |  | Requests one instance may have open at once. |
| `off` | bool |  | No rate limiting. The default in dev mode unless rate_limits is set. |

Owned by [Firewall](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/firewall).

#### `s3redirect:`

Signed S3 redirects for file downloads: enabled, URL lifetime. The --s3Redirect and --s3RedirectTTL flags win.

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | bool |  | On unless false (it only acts when S3 file storage is on). Flag: --s3Redirect. |
| `ttl` | duration |  | How long each signed URL stays valid. Default 5m, max 7 days. Flag: --s3RedirectTTL. |

Owned by [S3 Redirect](https://pocketone.dev/docs/extensions/s3redirect).

#### `server:`

How the binary listens: http, https and CORS origins (single-app mode: the serve command's defaults).

| Key | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `http` | string |  | Plain HTTP address, such as 127.0.0.1:8090. Single app: the --http default (the flag wins). Many instances: redirects to https when https is set. |
| `https` | string |  | HTTPS address. Single app: the --https default (the flag wins). Many instances: the main address. |
| `origins` | list of string |  | Allowed CORS origins. Single app: the --origins default (the flag wins). |
| `plain` | list of string |  | Many instances only: extra plain HTTP addresses with no redirect. |
| `tls.cert` | string |  | Many instances only: the certificate file, reloaded when it changes. |
| `tls.key` | string |  | Many instances only: the private key file, reloaded when it changes. |
| `shutdown_timeout` | duration |  | Many instances only: how long in-flight requests get to finish at stop. |

# PocketBase docs

PocketOne doesn't change how PocketBase itself works, so its docs are the reference for everything outside the
extensions. This site doesn't copy them.

- [Introduction](https://pocketbase.io/docs/)
- [Collections](https://pocketbase.io/docs/collections/)
- [API rules and filters](https://pocketbase.io/docs/api-rules-and-filters/)
- [Authentication](https://pocketbase.io/docs/authentication/)
- [Files upload and handling](https://pocketbase.io/docs/files-handling/)
- [Working with relations](https://pocketbase.io/docs/working-with-relations/)
- [Extend with JavaScript](https://pocketbase.io/docs/js-overview/)
- [Extend with Go](https://pocketbase.io/docs/go-overview/)
- [Going to production](https://pocketbase.io/docs/going-to-production/)
- [Web APIs reference](https://pocketbase.io/docs/api-records/)

PocketOne is built on PocketBase v0.41. When the docs there describe a newer release, some of it may not be in
PocketOne yet.
